labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

VS Code extension

### What feature would you like to see?

Feature request: Better conversation management, keyboard navigation, and UI customization in the Codex VS Code extension
I’m a long-time user of the Codex VS Code extension. I regularly manage multiple conversations and rely on keyboard shortcuts to switch between them and navigate long discussions.
I’ve implemented the following improvements through local patches to make these workflows more efficient. I’d love to see them supported natively, ideally through configurable options, so I no longer need to maintain and reapply patches after extension updates.
The colors, dimensions, and shortcuts below reflect my current preferences; they could be configurable rather than fixed defaults.
1. Visual customization — make information easier to distinguish
   - User message bubbles: Allow customization of the background and text colors of user messages. I currently use a WeChat-style green background with black text, which makes my messages easier to distinguish from assistant responses.
   - Conversation list: Display the running status, title, and timestamp in separate columns. Use a more distinctive color for the activity spinner; I currently use dark yellow.
   - Simplified interface: Provide an option to hide decorative icons on the sidebar home screen and use a fixed label, codex, for the conversation editor tab.
2. Layout and sizing — make better use of available space
   - Conversation list height: Allow larger sidebar lists and recent-conversation popovers. My current maximum heights are 600px for the sidebar list, 540px for the popover, and 80vh for the inner scrolling list.
   - List row layout: Adjust row spacing and title width to make long titles easier to read. Ensure that the selection outline around the current conversation is not clipped.
   - Conversation title button: Let the button at the top resize to fit its title, up to half the window width. Give it a larger clickable area and a clear keyboard focus indicator.
3. Workflow improvements — reduce the effort of switching and searching
   - Persistent, complete conversation list in the sidebar: Keep the full conversation list readily available, with search and filtering. List updates should not steal focus from the input field.
   - Quick access to recent conversations: Provide a configurable keyboard shortcut to toggle the recent-conversation popover while viewing a conversation. I currently use Ctrl/Cmd+W. When opened, the popover should automatically scroll to the current conversation.
   - Conversation sorting: Support a sorting mode that sorts the 14 most recent conversations by their full titles, followed by the remaining conversations in reverse chronological order. This makes it easier to organize frequently used conversations by title.
   - Letter shortcuts for quick selection: Allow the first eight conversations in the popover to be selected using q w e a s d x c. Disable these shortcuts while typing in the search field.
   - Reuse a single editor tab: When switching conversations from the list, reuse the same editor tab and Webview. Keep the selected conversation in the list synchronized with the conversation currently displayed.
   - Keyboard navigation: Support arrow keys, Page Up/Page Down, and Cmd+↑/↓ in the conversation list. Within the conversation body, support scrolling by approximately one screen at a time and jumping to the top or bottom.
   - Search within a conversation: Add a search button next to the conversation title and support Ctrl/Cmd+F. Typing a query should highlight matches without changing the reading position; pressing Enter should navigate to a result.
   - Archived conversations and title copying: Provide access to archived conversations through Settings. Add a button to copy a conversation’s full title from the conversation list, retain the ability to select title text with the mouse for copying, and show clear success or failure feedback.
   - Fork/Branch workflow: When creating a branch from a conversation in the editor, keep the parent conversation open instead of automatically switching to the new branch. Preserve the native (2)/(3) naming suffixes and include the full branch titles when sorting conversations.
These improvements would make the extension more comfortable for users who manage many conversations and rely heavily on keyboard navigation. Could you consider adding them as native features or configurable options in upcoming releases?

### Additional information

_No response_

items.title: Allow live context-limit changes mid-thread: select → compact if needed → apply

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: context
labels.description: Issues related to context management (including compaction)

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

items.body:
## Request

Add a **live context-limit selector** to Codex Desktop (and ideally CLI) that works **during an existing conversation**, without restarting or editing `config.toml`.

**Interaction:** select a supported context size or profile → Codex shows the effective limit and current usage → **if the current context exceeds the selected limit, prompt to compact now** → confirm and continue in the same thread.

### Expected behavior

- Allow increasing or decreasing the context limit mid-session, within what the current model/plan actually supports.
- On an increase, continue the thread without compaction when possible; don't silently claim extra capacity that the backend doesn't provide.
- On a decrease, if current context won't fit, offer **“Compact and apply”** (or cancel). Prefer preserving the active task, critical constraints and architecture decisions.
- Show the effective context window, current occupancy and resulting auto-compaction threshold *before* applying changes.
- Preserve conversation/task continuity and any project files. If the selected limit cannot be applied live, clearly explain why and offer the nearest supported option; don't silently alter the value.
- Prefer a simple dropdown + confirmation rather than requiring the user to close Codex, edit TOML and restart.

### Example UX

**Context:** Auto · 256K · 512K · 1M (show only options actually supported for the model/plan)

After choosing a smaller limit:
> Current context exceeds the selected capacity. **Compact and switch** / Cancel

After choosing a larger limit:
> This thread can use the selected capacity. **Apply** / Cancel

### Why

Context needs change *during* a project, not just when starting a thread. Users should be able to switch to a larger window before a complex refactor, or a smaller one for a lighter phase, without disrupting a long-running session.

Related: #40429 requests a per-thread profile selector and mentions editing the profile later. This issue focuses specifically on a **live, in-thread apply/compact-if-needed transition** and its confirmation/failure behavior. #50320 requests workflow-aware adaptive compaction; this is a simpler manual control that would complement it.

Environment (verified)

- The app update checker reports up_to_date.
- Earlier verified version: 26.928.31416, build 12553.
- Report date: 2026-10-02, Asia/Seoul.

Impact
Browser/Computer Use cannot initialize. Failure occurs before browser inventory,
page navigation, or any website request. Website HTTP errors are a separate issue.
Read-only shell diagnostics using an approved escalated execution path still work;
this is not a claim that every execution path is unavailable.

Reproduction on this existing installation
1. Open a local chat in the Windows desktop app.
2. Reset the Browser Use JavaScript kernel.
3. Run the documented entry point: await cua.getState();
4. The node_repl kernel exits before returning browser inventory.
5. Restart/reopen the app and repeat; failure persists.
Reproduction of the underlying state on a clean installation has not been established.

Observed tool error
node_repl kernel exited unexpectedly
kernel_status: exited(code=1)
kernel_stderr_tail: windows sandbox failed: helper_unknown_error: setup refresh had errors
reason: stdout_eof

Observed setup_error.json
{"code":"helper_unknown_error","message":"setup refresh had errors"}

Relevant sandbox log (personal path anonymized)
At 2026-10-02T14:19:06Z (2026-10-02 23:19:06 KST), setup refresh reported:
runtime read/execute validation failed: validate runtime read/execute access on
%LOCALAPPDATA%\OpenAI\Codex\runtimes\cua_node\be2aaea167c12e53\bin\node_repl.exe:
CreateFileW failed for the same file.
setup refresh completed with errors.

Read-only filesystem observations
- The target executable exists; metadata reports size 34,047,944 bytes and Archive attribute.
- A direct attempt to open that executable for reading returned Access to the path is denied.
- Querying the executable's ACL with Get-Acl/icacls also returned Access Denied.
- Parent runtime and bin directory ACLs were readable and showed inherited
  ReadAndExecute for CodexSandboxUsers and FullControl for the current user,
  SYSTEM and Administrators. This does not establish the executable's effective ACL.
- The root cause of the access denial has not been determined.
- The validator's CreateFileW log does not include the underlying numeric Windows error.

Recovery already attempted
- JavaScript kernel reset and fresh Browser Use initialization: failure persists.
- Full app exit and reopen: user reported doing this; subsequent calls still fail.
- Windows app Repair: user reported completion; subsequent calls still fail.
- App update from 26.928.31416 to 26.930.21537: verified, failure persists.
- An earlier direct @oai/sky initialization also failed before package initialization
  with the same kernel/sandbox startup error.
- No ACL/security changes, runtime deletion, app Reset, or sandbox weakening performed.

Potentially related existing reports (same root cause NOT established)
- https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/49433
  Similar node_repl.exe access denial. This report does NOT establish whether our
  runtime is stale or mismatched with current configuration.
- https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/50268
  Same validation error family but a different, long dependency-directory target.

Request to maintainers
Please investigate runtime file access validation and advise a supported recovery
that preserves projects, chat history, configuration and sandbox protections.
Please include the Windows GetLastError code/message in runtime validation errors
so access denial, missing paths and other failures can be distinguished.

Privacy review
This draft includes no full session transcript, business/customer data, screenshots,
credentials, tokens, account name, device name or unredacted personal paths.
No .sandbox-secrets contents were read or included. Raw logs are not attached.

items.title: Feature request: workflow-aware adaptive compaction based on next task's context needs

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: context
labels.description: Issues related to context management (including compaction)

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

items.body:
## Summary

Introduce **workflow-aware adaptive compaction** for Codex (desktop and CLI). Instead of primarily compacting when a fixed fraction of the context window is reached, Codex should plan a context budget around the **next expected unit of work**, choose a safe compaction range at an appropriate task boundary, and selectively preserve the engineering knowledge the next workflow requires.

This is especially important for large, long-running projects: source files persist on disk, but the reasoning behind architectural decisions, rejected approaches, inter-module dependencies, and unresolved debugging observations may exist only in the conversation.

## Problem

A single compaction threshold treats very different workloads alike. A routine bug fix may need little additional context; a multi-file architectural refactor or full codebase audit may need substantially more. Compacting mid-refactor can discard working knowledge at the point where it matters most. Keeping everything indefinitely also has costs: stale tool outputs and obsolete exploratory paths compete with relevant context.

Increasing the context window helps but does not solve the scheduling and information-selection problem. A large context window is not durable project memory.

## Proposed design

1. **Forecast the next workflow.** At a natural phase boundary (e.g., investigation -> implementation, implementation -> validation), estimate the context likely required for the next phase. Use a **range with uncertainty**, not a fixed token allocation. Consider known files, expected tool calls, planned steps, and observed usage from comparable prior phases. When the next phase is unknown, maintain conservative headroom and revise forecasts as the plan develops.

2. **Reserve capacity, then decide.** Compare current active context plus the forecast range and safety margin against the *effective* model/session limit (not a user-entered value that may exceed what is actually available). If the next phase fits, avoid unnecessary compaction. Otherwise plan selective compaction **before** entering that phase, ideally at a clean handoff. Reassess incrementally as the workflow evolves.

3. **Compact by relevance and scope.** Separate context into:
   - **Must preserve:** current objective, user constraints, accepted architectural decisions and rationale, module relationships, verified discoveries, unresolved risks, next actions and validation criteria.
   - **Retrievable:** project files, versioned design docs, Git history, previous tool outputs and archived investigation details with pointers/provenance.
   - **Candidates for compression:** obsolete logs, duplicate reads, abandoned exploratory paths and completed phase minutiae.
   Preserve selected sections at full fidelity where possible; compress specific completed phases rather than flattening the entire conversation indiscriminately.

4. **Create a verifiable handoff.** At compaction, produce a structured checkpoint identifying what was preserved, what was compressed, which decisions remain binding, where supporting evidence can be reloaded, and which assumptions need confirmation. Do not treat a generated summary as proof of factual correctness; check against project artifacts where feasible. Support targeted restoration of archived details.

5. **Avoid dangerous moments.** Prefer phase boundaries over a mid-operation threshold. Keep an unavoidable hard safety limit and fallback behavior for sudden large tool responses, model-limit changes, poor forecasts, or unknown future workflows. No proposal should bypass the model's real maximum context capacity.

6. **Expose clear controls in Codex Desktop.** Display the effective context limit, current utilization, projected headroom for the upcoming workflow and imminent compaction reason. Offer Auto (workflow-aware), Manual/Review, and simpler legacy automatic behavior. Let users pin important instructions or request a checkpoint, without implying any form of perfect memory.

## Example

In a 700K-effective-token session, suppose the current active context is 470K, leaving 230K available (illustrative numbers only).
- The next small fix is estimated to require 20–40K: proceed without compaction.
- A major refactor is estimated to require 140–190K plus a safety margin: preserve the active working context if feasible and complete that phase before revisiting compaction.
- A repo-wide audit is estimated to need 250–350K: create a checkpoint, prune stale completed-phase logs, preserve architectural decisions and reserve enough context *before* starting the audit.

The decision depends on workflow requirements, confidence and effective capacity—not a universal 25%, 50% or 75% trigger.

## Evaluation / acceptance criteria

- Lower rate of compaction interrupting an unfinished logical phase.
- Better post-compaction retention of user constraints, architecture decisions and verified debugging findings (evaluated on multi-session engineering benchmarks).
- Fewer repeated file reads, repeated failed approaches and unnecessary re-investigations after compaction.
- Comparable or better task success and cost/latency than fixed-threshold compaction under matched workloads.
- User-visible explanations when the planner compacts early, defers compaction or invokes an emergency fallback.

## Related requests

This proposal complements, rather than duplicates:
- #15848 — phase-boundary compaction.
- #41538 — adaptive context-budget expansion based on compaction outcomes.
- #36669 — model-callable selective context management.

The additional request here is **forecasting the next workflow to determine an adaptive compaction range and preservation policy before work begins**, with a reliable project-state checkpoint and visible effective-capacity reporting.

Feature concept submitted at a user's request; illustrative budgets are examples, not measured Codex behavior.

macOS 26.6.2 (build 25G83), Apple Silicon. `uname -mprs`: `Darwin 25.6.0 arm64 arm`.

I have encountered several unexpected voice-chat starts in the desktop app while working on other things, first noticed on October 1–2, 2026. The apparent trigger is Ctrl+Shift+V, which I use to paste in the terminal view of my dot's cloud computer.

The [official macOS command reference](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/reference/commands) assigns Ctrl+Shift+V to “Start voice chat”. My intended action in this workflow is terminal paste; I do not intend to start a voice conversation.

The following is a minimal workflow to check the suspected conflict. A controlled reproduction has not yet been performed:

1. Open a dot's cloud-computer terminal view in the macOS desktop app.
2. Keep the default Ctrl+Shift+V binding for “Start voice chat”.
3. Copy a harmless short string, such as `voice-shortcut-test`, and focus the terminal input.
4. Press Ctrl+Shift+V to paste.
5. Check whether a voice chat starts unexpectedly and whether the terminal receives the pasted text.

The observed symptom is an unexpected voice-chat start. The precise original keypress and terminal focus were not recorded, and I have not established whether paste also occurs. I have not reproduced this in a fresh profile.

When interacting with the dot's cloud-computer terminal, I should be able to use its paste shortcut without unintentionally starting a voice chat. Shortcut handling should respect the active terminal or otherwise avoid this collision.

- The shortcut configuration inspected during the investigation contained no custom override for the voice-start shortcut. This does not rule out every individual configuration influence.
- Removing or changing the voice shortcut is a possible workaround; its effectiveness has not yet been verified here.
- Related reports: [#36896](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/36896) concerns the Windows desktop app's integrated terminal with WSL2; [#35418](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/35418) concerns plain-text paste in the Windows composer. ### What issue are you seeing?

- The assistant reported that `node_repl` was unavailable.

- The assistant could not control the mouse, keyboard, or application windows.

4. Ask whether Computer Use is available in the session.
5. The assistant reports that the required `node_repl` tool is missing. Shell commands remain available, but mouse, keyboard, and application control are unavailable.

The permissions selector should remain available after a chat starts.

ChatGPT Work에서 시작한 작업이 Codex → 클라우드에서는 완료되어 최종 답변과 결과 파일까지 확인됩니다. 그러나 작업을 시작한 원래 Work 대화에는 완료 답변이 표시되지 않고, 작업 중 타이머가 다음 날까지 계속 증가합니다.

발생 과정

10월 1일 09:11에 ChatGPT Work 대화에서 작업을 시작했습니다.

같은 대화에서 09:24에 재검토를 요청했습니다.

결과가 보이지 않아 같은 대화에서 “얼마나 남았어?”, “얼마나 더 해야해?” 등의 상태 확인 질문을 보냈습니다. 이 후속 대화는 Codex에서 다른 작업으로 분류되어 보입니다.

이후 마지막 답변의 “새 채팅에서 이어가기” 기능으로 새 브랜치를 만들었습니다. 결과 누락과 타이머 문제는 브랜치를 만들기 전부터 발생했습니다.

10월 2일에도 작업 중 타이머가 계속 증가하고 있었습니다.

화면별 불일치

items.title: Guardian silently omits `auto_review.extra_policy` with the current codex-auto-review catalog template

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: sandbox
labels.description: Issues related to permissions or sandboxing

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: config
labels.description: Issues involving config.toml, config keys, config merging, or config updates

items.body:
### What version of Codex CLI is running?

codex-cli 0.160.0

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Pro 200

### Which model were you using?

gpt-6.1-sol

### What platform is your computer?

Darwin 27.0.0 arm64 arm

### What terminal emulator and version are you using (if applicable)?

Ghostty

### Codex doctor report

```json

```

### What issue are you seeing?

A nonblank `[auto_review].extra_policy` is accepted, but its text is silently omitted from the synchronous Guardian reviewer's base instructions when the selected `codex-auto-review` catalog entry supplies a policy template without `{{ extra_policy }}`. `[auto_review].policy` and `experimental_policy_template` are unset.

The [configuration reference](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/config-file/config-reference) describes `extra_policy` as additional policy included alongside the main policy. The current catalog template prevents that insertion. The renderer provides no missing-placeholder diagnostic. The catalog's base security policy is retained, but the configured additional rules are absent.

Observed evidence:

- A fresh catalog fetched by the official 0.160.0 binary at `2026-10-02T06:06:03.097223Z` has zero `{{ extra_policy }}` placeholders in the `codex-auto-review` template
- Executing the 0.160.0 Rust renderer body with that fresh template and a neutral extra-policy sentinel produces zero sentinel occurrences. The bundled-template control produces one occurrence. Both preserve the full base policy

Verification establishes omitted prompt input. Action enforcement outcomes were not tested. Catalog contents may vary by account or server rollout. These observations concern the catalog served to this account.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Configure automatic review with a nonblank additional policy in a test Codex home:

   ```toml
   model = "gpt-6.1-sol"
   approval_policy = "on-request"
   approvals_reviewer = "auto_review"
   sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"

   [auto_review]
   extra_policy = "EXTRA_POLICY_SENTINEL: Require explicit confirmation before writing guardian-policy-probe.txt."
   ```

   Leave `auto_review.policy` and `auto_review.experimental_policy_template` unset.

2. Sign in normally and fetch the model catalog:

   ```sh
   codex --version
   codex debug models > catalog.json
   ```

   For a fresh server fetch, use a test Codex home with no existing `models_cache.json`. In 0.160.0, `debug models` uses `OnlineIfUncached`, so an existing cache can otherwise be reused.

3. Inspect the actual selected catalog template and reproduce its rendering with this source-equivalent checker:

   ```sh
   uv run --offline --no-project python - catalog.json <<'PY'
   import json
   import sys

   with open(sys.argv[1]) as file:
       models = json.load(file)["models"]
   model = next(model for model in models if model["slug"] == "codex-auto-review")
   messages = model["model_messages"]["auto_review"]
   template = messages["policy_template"]
   policy = messages["policy"]
   extra = "EXTRA_POLICY_SENTINEL: Require explicit confirmation before writing guardian-policy-probe.txt."
   prompt = policy.strip().join(
       part.replace("{{ extra_policy }}", extra.strip())
       for part in template.rstrip().split("{{ tenant_policy_config }}")
   )
   rendered = f"{prompt}\n\nReview contract.\n"
   print("extra_policy placeholders:", template.count("{{ extra_policy }}"))
   print("extra_policy sentinel occurrences:", rendered.count("EXTRA_POLICY_SENTINEL"))
   print("full base policy present:", policy.strip() in rendered)
   PY
   ```

   Observed output:

   ```text
   extra_policy placeholders: 0
   extra_policy sentinel occurrences: 0
   full base policy present: True
   ```

   This checker mirrors `GuardianPolicyInstructions::body` in 0.160.0. It is a deterministic rendering reproduction, independent of model behavior. I also executed the original Rust renderer body in an isolated harness with the same results. Substituting the release's bundled `policy_template.md` changes the sentinel count to `1`.

4. For optional end-to-end confirmation, start a new CLI session with that configuration and request a harmless read-only command that requires approval review, such as `pwd` through `exec_command` with `sandbox_permissions = "require_escalated"`. Confirm a Guardian rollout was created and inspect its `session_meta.payload.base_instructions.text` for `EXTRA_POLICY_SENTINEL`.

   This inference-based confirmation has not been performed. The verified reproduction above uses the fresh catalog and the release renderer with the neutral sentinel.

### What is the expected behavior?

When `auto_review.extra_policy` is nonblank, normal automatic-review prompt construction should include it alongside the resolved base policy, including when `codex-auto-review` supplies the template through the model catalog.

If a selected template cannot include the configured policy, the CLI should surface that incompatibility instead of silently proceeding with the policy omitted. Users should be able to keep `auto_review.policy` unset and retain the catalog's base policy while adding local rules through the documented setting.

### Additional information

The failure occurs at the boundary between the client renderer and the catalog-provided template:

1. [Configuration loading](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.160.0/codex-rs/core/src/config/mod.rs#L4029-L4048) resolves nonblank `extra_policy` into `guardian_extra_policy`, with managed precedence
2. [Catalog message resolution](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.160.0/codex-rs/prompts/src/model_messages/guardian.rs#L41-L43) prefers the supplied catalog template over the bundled template
3. [Reviewer setup](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.160.0/codex-rs/core/src/guardian/reviewer_config.rs#L31-L47) passes the resolved extra policy and selected template to `GuardianPolicyInstructions`
4. [The renderer](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.160.0/codex-rs/prompts/src/guardian_instructions.rs#L54-L69) inserts additional policy only by replacing `{{ extra_policy }}`. A missing placeholder discards that input

The fetched catalog template differs from the release's bundled template only by the missing extra-policy slot:

```text
Catalog:
# Security Policy
{{ tenant_policy_config }}

# Investigation Guidelines

Bundled:
# Security Policy
{{ tenant_policy_config }}

{{ extra_policy }}

# Investigation Guidelines
```

[PR #47125](https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/47125), merged on 2026-09-21, explicitly added extra policy to both Guardian reviewer templates and Guardian v2 classification. Its implementation is not limited to a particular reviewer model. The reviewer path therefore already has support intended to compose this input. The missing catalog placeholder prevents that support from taking effect in the observed `codex-auto-review` configuration.

Two details explain the existing test coverage:

- [Integration scenario](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/26cb4d73e2ce25575644038d7af5beb2440d0ed0/codex-rs/core/tests/suite/scenarios_guardian_extra_policy.rs#L71-L78) explicitly overrides the reviewer template with the bundled one
- [Renderer unit test](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.160.0/codex-rs/prompts/src/guardian_instructions_tests.rs#L51-L55) explicitly expects omission when a nonblank extra policy is passed to a template without its slot

These tests cover insertion into a compatible template and the renderer's behavior with an incompatible one. They do not establish that the normal catalog-selected template includes the additional policy.

[PR #47287](https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/47287), merged on 2026-09-22, subsequently updated only this scenario's snapshot for retained user instructions. It did not change the template-selection or extra-policy rendering code.

A fix should align the served `codex-auto-review` template with the additional-policy contract and add coverage through catalog-template selection without forcing the bundled override. Client-side validation or a defined insertion fallback would also prevent this class of silent omission from recurring with an older or incompatible catalog template.

The scope here is synchronous reviewer prompt composition. [The Guardian v2 classifier path](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.160.0/codex-rs/ext/guardian-v2/src/async_scorer/config.rs#L290-L306) concatenates the base and extra policy before classifier rendering and truncation. It does not depend on this reviewer template's extra-policy placeholder.

[Issue #38316](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/38316) discusses local `auto_review.policy` replacing the base policy. This report uses `extra_policy` with `policy` unset. PR #47125 does not link #38316 as a closing issue or state that it was the reason for introducing the new field.

I searched public open and closed issues and PRs on 2026-10-02 for `extra_policy`, `guardian_extra_policy`, `extra-policy` with `template`, `Guardian` with `template`, and `codex-auto-review` with `policy`. I found #47125 and related policy/template discussions, but no report specifically describing the missing extra-policy placeholder in the served `codex-auto-review` template. This is a bounded public search.

items.title: Critical: multi-command exec_command batches hide earlier failures behind final-command status

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: tool-calls
labels.description: Issues related to tool calling

items.body:
### What issue are you seeing?

**Reported severity: critical.** Codex batches independent commands into a single `exec_command` shell invocation, but the result exposes one aggregate exit code. Successful reads followed by a failed read appear as a failed batch; more seriously, an earlier failed command followed by a successful command produces exit code 0.

During a real repository inspection, the agent combined multiple reads and searches. An absent `.npmrc` caused a final `rg` to return 2, and an absent sibling `AGENTS.md` caused a final `cat` to return 1. Other reads in those batches succeeded. The user had to ask which operations actually failed.

Follow-up, side-effect-free probes in the same Codex session confirmed that reversing the success/failure order can instead hide the earlier failure behind exit code 0. The shell is following normal shell semantics; the issue is Codex's command batching and failure accounting/reporting, not a request to change Bash semantics.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Run these as separate `exec_command` calls, each containing two newline-separated commands.

1. Successful command followed by failure:

```sh
printf '%s\n' 'first command succeeded'
false
```

Observed tool result:

```json
{"exit_code":1,"output":"first command succeeded\n"}
```

2. Failure followed by a successful command:

```sh
false
printf '%s\n' 'second command succeeded'
```

Observed tool result:

```json
{"exit_code":0,"output":"second command succeeded\n"}
```

Neither result provides a structured status for each component command. In the second case, the first command's failure produces no output and is absent from the aggregate success status.

The probes were invoked through Code Mode `functions.exec` using `tools.exec_command`; the outer script also completed normally while one nested command result had exit code 1. The nested exit code was present when explicitly printed, so this is not a claim that the raw nested result was lost.

### What is the expected behavior?

Codex should preserve and account for each relevant command's outcome when it chooses to batch commands. It should distinguish complete success, partial success, failure, and commands not run, and identify the failed step clearly.

For dependent operations, an earlier failure must prevent dependent work or remain an explicit failure in the result. For independent inspection operations, later reads may continue, but their successes must not erase an earlier failure or make the entire batch look as though every read failed. Merely adding fail-fast behavior everywhere would not address both cases.

### Additional information

- Environment: Linux, Bash, Codex shell tools through Code Mode.
- Local `codex --version`: `codex-cli 0.160.0`. This identifies the local CLI command, not an independently verified version of the serving runtime.
- Both minimal probes were executed and produced the results above; neither changed files.
- The original incident involved read-only inspection. No failed build, deployment, or data loss was observed. The critical concern is the same aggregation allowing an agent to treat an earlier failed prerequisite as success during consequential workflows.
- Existing issues were searched for multi-command execution, final-command exit status, and partial-success reporting; no exact duplicate was identified.

### Environment
- macOS (Apple Silicon), Codex TUI workers 0.157.1 / 0.159.2
- Managed app-server package selected at 0.160.0
- Shared app-server daemon; `~/.codex/app-server-daemon/settings.json` absent, so auto-update is on with the default 60-minute interval
- Several long-running TUI sessions attached (orchestrated workers, 40–90 min turns)

### Observed
The daemon received shutdown/drain signals at 2026-10-01 21:20:27Z, 21:31:52Z, 22:21:39Z and 23:22:50Z. The first one coincided with selection of 0.160.0; the later, roughly hourly drains happened with no new release.
Each replacement daemon came up and accepted `initialize` quickly, but the attached TUIs ended with:

```
Automatic reconnect could not restore this session
app-server session could not be restored
Reconnect failed — check the endpoint, then relaunch
```

The TUI processes stayed alive and their in-progress turns never completed. We lost three multi-hour sessions this way.

### Expected
A scheduled update check that has nothing new to install must not interrupt attached turns. After a daemon replacement, existing TUI sessions should resume their threads.

### Request
- Do not restart the daemon while turns are active, or defer the restart until it is idle.
- Make reconnect restore-aware across daemon replacement.
- Log the updater identity, the selected binary identity and the restart-mode decision, so a repeated hourly `Always` restart (updater/selected-binary digest mismatch that never settles after handoff) can be diagnosed.
- Document the supported opt-out (`updater.autoUpdateEnabled: false` in `settings.json`) and whether `daemon stop` also stops the updater.

Workaround that stopped the failures for us: `settings.json` with `"updater": {"autoUpdateEnabled": false}`, then `codex app-server daemon start` (updater stops, daemon not rotated), and launching worker TUIs with `--no-daemon`.

### What version of Codex CLI is running?

`codex-cli 0.160.0`

The managed app-server was still running Codex 0.158.0:

```text
cliVersion:          0.160.0
managedCodexVersion: 0.158.0
appServerVersion:    0.158.0
```

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Plus, signed in to Codex CLI with ChatGPT.

### Which model were you trying to use?

`gpt-6.1-sol`

### What platform is your computer?

WSL / Linux x86_64, using the official standalone Codex installation.

### What issue are you seeing?

GPT-6.1 Sol was already available for the same ChatGPT account in Codex Desktop, but it was not available in Codex CLI.

The CLI/app-server versions were out of sync: the CLI had been upgraded to 0.160.0, while the managed and running app-server remained on 0.158.0.

The stale daemon package was visible under:

```text
~/.codex/packages/app-server-daemon/current
```

and its binary reported:

```text
codex-cli 0.158.0
```

After cleaning/reinitializing the old local Codex state and signing in again using the official ChatGPT login flow, GPT-6.1 Sol immediately became available in Codex CLI.

This does not prove that every GPT-6.1 Sol availability problem is caused by app-server version skew, but it appears to be a useful diagnostic/workaround for at least some users who already have Sol access elsewhere on the same account.

### Suggested diagnostic/workaround

For users who have GPT-6.1 Sol in ChatGPT/Codex Desktop but not in Codex CLI, check:

```bash
codex --version
codex app-server daemon version
```

Compare:

```text
cliVersion
managedCodexVersion
appServerVersion
```

If the CLI is newer than the managed/running app-server, reconcile/update the daemon before assuming this is an account rollout or entitlement problem.

The CLI currently exposes a supported daemon update path, for example:

```bash
codex app-server daemon update
codex app-server daemon restart
codex app-server daemon version
```

If the local daemon state is stale or cannot be reconciled normally, reinitializing the local Codex state and signing in again was the workaround that resolved it in this case. Users should of course back up any local Codex state they need before removing it.

### Why this may matter for GPT-6.1 Sol reports

There are currently reports where GPT-6.1 Sol returns an unsupported-with-ChatGPT-account error, such as #49396.

There is also an existing report that managed app-server can remain on an older version after the CLI is upgraded: #49418.

My case appears to connect these two failure modes:

1. Same ChatGPT Plus account already had GPT-6.1 Sol in Codex Desktop.
2. Codex CLI was 0.160.0.
3. Managed/running app-server was still 0.158.0.
4. Sol was unavailable in the CLI.
5. After cleaning/reinitializing the stale local state and signing in again, Sol immediately appeared.

So for at least some "Sol is available in Desktop but missing in CLI" reports, checking app-server version skew may save users from waiting for an account rollout that has actually already reached them.

### Expected behavior

A Codex CLI upgrade should not silently leave a managed app-server on an older version when that version skew can affect behavior.

Ideally, Codex should either:

- automatically align the managed app-server with the upgraded CLI;
- prominently warn when `cliVersion != managedCodexVersion` or `cliVersion != appServerVersion`; and/or
- surface this mismatch prominently in `codex doctor` when troubleshooting model availability.

Related: #49396, #49418.

```json
app_server.status: warning (background server socket is stale or unreachable at report capture time)
Other warnings: optional MCP configuration issues, rollout/state DB inventory differences, TERM=dumb in the non-interactive diagnostic run.
```

Immediately after the manual workaround, daemon version/start reported the server running on 0.160.0. The later doctor socket warning is recorded here separately; its relationship to the updater failure is unknown.

### What issue are you seeing?

Updating the local Windows background server fails and leaves it on an older version than the installed CLI.

The /daemon update action reports:
```text
Updating the local background server...
Error: standalone Codex updater exited with status exit code: 1
Error: Daemon update failed with status exit code: 1
```

Running the update directly exposes a more specific error:
```powershell
codex app-server daemon update --from-cli --yes
```
```text
Error: Zugriff verweigert (os error 5)
```
(English: Access denied.)

Observed version mismatches:
- CLI 0.159.3 / managed daemon 0.157.0 on Oct 1, 2026.
- CLI 0.160.0 / managed daemon 0.159.3 on Oct 2, 2026.

The first mismatch coincided with GPT-6.1 Sol missing from the Windows CLI model picker, although it was available in WSL and the Windows app. Updating the daemon manually restored the model choice (confirmed afterward).

The exact failing filesystem operation and root cause have not been identified.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Observed on this existing native Windows npm installation (not yet reproduced on a clean installation):

1. Have a managed background server installed/running at an older version than the CLI.
2. Update the npm-installed CLI; verify with `codex --version`.
3. Try updating the background server via `/daemon`. It fails with updater/daemon exit code 1.
4. Run `codex app-server daemon update --from-cli --yes` in PowerShell. It fails with `Zugriff verweigert (os error 5)`.
5. Run `codex app-server daemon version`: the CLI is newer, but the managed/running server remains on the old version.

For the 0.157.0 -> 0.159.3 attempt, stopping the server with `codex app-server daemon stop` before retrying did not resolve the error.

Please note that the second failure happened after the manual junction workaround described below. The first failure predated that workaround.

### What is the expected behavior?

The daemon updater should install the selected CLI package and restart the managed server successfully, bringing the CLI and daemon versions into agreement. If an operation fails, the error should identify the affected path/operation so the cause can be diagnosed, rather than exposing only exit code 1 through /daemon.

### Additional information

Installation: global npm package @openai/codex on native Windows. CODEX_HOME uses the default %USERPROFILE%\.codex.

Checks during investigation:
- The installation directory was writable under the current Windows user.
- The install.lock file could be opened for exclusive read/write access and then closed.
- Copying the same CLI vendor package into the managed daemon releases directory succeeded.
- These checks do not prove that every operation performed by the updater has the required access.

Manual workaround used twice:
1. Copy the installed npm CLI's vendor package into `%USERPROFILE%\.codex\packages\app-server-daemon\releases\<version>-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`.
2. Verify the copied executable's version.
3. Stop the managed daemon.
4. Rename the existing `current` directory junction to a backup junction, preserving the old release.
5. Create a new `current` junction targeting the copied release and update the `auto-update-version` marker to the matching release identifier.
6. Start the daemon and verify the CLI, managed package, and running server versions agree.

This brought the server to 0.159.3 and later 0.160.0. The original releases/backup junctions remain available; this is a workaround, not a fix to the updater.

No clean-install reproduction or confirmed root cause yet. No thread ID included because the failing operation is daemon management, not a model turn.

items.body:
## Summary

After updating the ChatGPT/Codex desktop app to 26.930.21537 (build 12776; bundled Codex CLI 0.159.0-alpha.12.1), an existing custom Responses provider stopped contributing its Codex-native model catalog. Existing chats using `gpt-6.1-sol` displayed `Custom` in the model picker, and the user observed `High` effort. Sol 6.1 disappeared from the picker. The same provider/configuration still returns the full catalog with CLI 0.149.1.

## Environment and configuration

- macOS arm64
- Desktop: 26.930.21537 / 12776
- Bundled CLI: 0.159.0-alpha.12.1
- Previously working standalone CLI: 0.149.1
- Local Responses gateway: CLIProxyAPI v8.0.8, managed by Quotio
- The gateway's authenticated `/v1/models?client_version=0.159.0-alpha.12.1` returns HTTP 200 with a Codex-native top-level `models` array containing 32 models, including `gpt-6.1-sol` with `visibility: list` and supported reasoning efforts.

Relevant existing configuration (token omitted):

```toml
model = "gpt-6-astra"
model_reasoning_effort = "high"
model_provider = "cliproxyapi"

[model_providers.cliproxyapi]
name = "OpenAI"
base_url = "http://127.0.0.1:8317/v1"
wire_api = "responses"
requires_openai_auth = true
supports_websockets = true
experimental_bearer_token = "<local-gateway-token>"
```

Existing chats separately retain `gpt-6.1-sol` selections. No custom `model_catalog_json` is configured.

## Reproduction and observed results

Run `codex debug models` with each binary against the same configuration:

| Case | Catalog size | `gpt-6.1-sol` present |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Gateway catalog endpoint | 32 | Yes |
| CLI 0.149.1 | 32 | Yes |
| Bundled CLI 0.159.0-alpha.12.1 | 10 | No |
| New CLI `debug models --bundled` | 10 | No |
| New CLI with only explicit `model_catalog_url` override | 10 | No |
| New CLI with only `features.api_key_model_discovery=true` override | 10 | No |
| New CLI with both overrides | 32 | Yes |

The desktop logs on resuming several existing chats contain:

```text
Unknown model gpt-6.1-sol is used. This will use fallback model metadata.
```

This is not a gateway 401 or missing-model response. The authenticated catalog call succeeds. The older cached catalog also contained the missing model. The new runtime's result exactly matches its bundled catalog.

The `Custom` label is user-visible. The scope of the reported effort fallback is not yet established: one inspected chat retained its stored `low` effort in later settings events, with an intervening `high` settings event. This report does not claim every saved chat effort was permanently overwritten.

## Verified workaround

```toml
[model_providers.cliproxyapi]
# other provider fields retained
model_catalog_url = "http://127.0.0.1:8317/v1/models"

[features]
api_key_model_discovery = true
```

Both temporary command-line overrides and these persisted settings restore the full catalog in the bundled runtime. The feature is currently labelled `under development`. Desktop picker verification after restart is pending; the workaround is verified at the bundled runtime's model-catalog boundary.

## Suspected compatibility boundary

In the public rust-v0.159.0 source, `OpenAiModelsManager::refresh_available_models` treats a provider bearer token as API-key authentication and returns before cache/network discovery unless API-key model discovery is enabled and supported. `OpenAiModelsEndpoint::supports_api_key_models` requires an explicit catalog URL for a custom base URL. That appears to silently change the behavior of the existing configuration above, even with `requires_openai_auth = true`.

Please confirm whether this is intended. If so, an upgrade migration or actionable warning for previously working custom-provider catalogs would prevent existing chats from silently losing model metadata and picker options. The UI should also preserve the chat's stored reasoning effort when its model temporarily lacks catalog metadata.

No account identifiers, credentials, or conversation contents are included.

items.title: Codex hooks receive session CWD instead of explicit tool workdir, blocking documented release workflows

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: model-behavior
labels.description: Issues related to behaviors exhibited by the model

labels.name: hooks
labels.description: Issues related to event hooks

items.body:
## Summary

Codex did not reliably follow an explicit repository release procedure from a detailed `AGENTS.md` / release document, then its PreToolUse hook received the supervisor workspace as `cwd` instead of the command's effective `workdir`. Together, that blocked the canonical release command and encouraged an incorrect fallback.

This is a report about agent execution and hook-context fidelity, not a request to change a third-party tool.

## Observed behavior

- The repository documented one canonical release command for a versioned environment package. It also documented two mutually exclusive delivery channels: a Git/bare-hub slipstream path and an npm-installed-package path.
- Codex was run in a supervisor workspace but invoked the canonical command with a different explicit `workdir` (the environment package worktree).
- The Codex PreToolUse payload continued to identify the supervisor workspace as `cwd`.
- A repository guard that correctly checks completion claims against the repository being shipped therefore judged the canonical release as a foreign claim and included unrelated dirty files from the supervisor workspace.
- Instead of stopping and reporting the guard-context defect, Codex selected an alternate land command. That command landed Git but did not perform the documented publish/install transaction.
- Codex then incorrectly tried direct npm installation even though the docs stated the active target was a bare-hub slipstream. The correct sequence was only followed after an operator correction.

## Expected behavior

1. A command launched with an explicit workdir should expose that effective workdir to every Codex hook, or expose it separately and unambiguously from the session workspace.
2. Before a release/deploy/publish action, Codex should give explicit repository instructions higher priority than inferred topology or a convenient alternate command.
3. When a guard blocks the documented canonical operation because execution context is inconsistent, Codex should surface that mismatch and stop. It should not select a fallback whose release semantics differ.
4. Codex should make the repository/worktree it believes a command affects visible in the action trace, so a human can detect a context mismatch before an external change.

## Minimal reproduction shape

1. Start Codex in workspace `A` with a PreToolUse hook that consumes `cwd` and gates a release command against a work contract for repository `B`.
2. Execute a release command with the tool `workdir` set to repository `B`.
3. Observe that the hook receives `cwd=A` rather than `cwd=B`.
4. The guard misclassifies the release as foreign or associates it with unrelated dirty state in `A`.

## Why this matters

The repository instructions were unusually explicit and structurally sound. The failure was not a missing instruction or operator error. A system that accepts repository-level procedures but can silently substitute a different workspace context at hook time makes guarded release workflows unreliable: the safe path is blocked and a less-safe path appears available.

## Requested outcome

- Preserve the effective tool workdir in hook payloads.
- Add an integration test for a session workspace different from the tool workdir.
- Add an agent-side guardrail: if an explicit documented release command is blocked by a workspace/context mismatch, report that mismatch rather than choosing a semantically different release command.

A completely new Codex chat becomes unable to deliver messages after only one or two turns, even after fully quitting and restarting VS Code and using only one intended Codex session.

The UI reports:

`Delivery could not be confirmed. Check the conversation before deleting this saved message`

Messages disappear after pressing Enter, later return to the composer, or appear as `Steering` although no agent turn is running.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Fully quit VS Code with Cmd+Q.
2. Start VS Code.
3. Open one workspace and the Codex extension.
4. Create a completely new Codex chat.
5. Send an initial prompt and wait for completion.
6. Send one or two follow-up prompts.

## Actual behavior

The chat becomes unreliable or unusable. Retrying does not reliably recover it. Creating another new chat only works briefly before the same failure returns.

## Expected behavior

The new chat should retain one valid writer. Each submitted follow-up should either start a turn or return a stable, actionable error without losing or misclassifying the message.

## Correlated log timeline

Affected new conversation/thread: `01a0fc01-dc0b-7832-b08a-ec1edfd4653b`

```text
2026-10-02 11:47:31.193 Conversation created; usedPrewarmedThread=true
2026-10-02 11:52:52.487 maybe_resume_started; previousResumeState=needs_resume; previousStreamRole=null
2026-10-02 11:52:53.916 thread_stream_role_changed; previousRole=null; role=owner
2026-10-02 11:52:53.933 maybe_resume_success; assignedStreamRole=owner; turnCount=1
2026-10-02 11:53:39 Failed to create session: thread-store conflict: thread 01a0fc01-dc0b-7832-b08a-ec1edfd4653b already has an active writer
2026-10-02 11:53:39.878 Failed to release queued message send lock; errorMessage="\"undefined\" is not valid JSON"; errorName=SyntaxError
```

The persistence error identifies RPC method `thread/resume`, transport `stdio`, client `VS Code`, and client version `26.930.21537`.

- This is not limited to an old or previously shared thread. The example thread was newly created at 11:47:31.
- The thread is successfully assigned `role=owner` before the later self-conflict.
- The same pattern has occurred across several conversation IDs.
- Fully quitting VS Code, using one intended Codex session, creating new chats, avoiding duplicate windows, and retrying did not resolve it.
- The `JSON.parse(undefined)` failure appears to prevent cleanup of the queued-message send lock.

## Suspected component

The extension appears to initiate a competing `thread/resume` after already becoming owner. This may involve prewarmed threads, retained webviews, thread hydration, or a race between hydration and composer submission.

After the writer conflict, the error-handling path attempts to parse an undefined response and fails to release the send lock.

Please investigate:

1. Why the same VS Code extension lifecycle initiates a competing `thread/resume` after becoming owner.
2. Whether a prewarmed thread or retained webview keeps a hidden writer alive.
3. Whether thread hydration and composer submission can race.
4. Why send-lock cleanup calls `JSON.parse` on an undefined value.

## What version of Codex CLI is running?

`codex-cli 0.159.3`, beim Erstellen dieser Meldung lokal geprüft. Die genaue Version jedes früheren Turns ist nicht separat rekonstruiert.

## What subscription do you have?

Ich hatte ein OpenAI-Abo für **200 USD pro Monat**. **Aufgrund genau dieses Vorfalls habe ich dieses Abo gekündigt.**

## Which model were you using?

**Sol 6.1 mit Reasoning high**: `gpt-6.1-sol`, `model_reasoning_effort = "high"`.

Diese Einstellung ist beim Erstellen der Meldung in der lokalen Codex-Konfiguration bestätigt. Sie beschreibt den gemeldeten Codex-Leitungspfad; nicht alle beteiligten Implementierungs- und Reviewagenten nutzten dasselbe Modell. Es wird keine nachträgliche, vollständige Modellverifikation sämtlicher historischer Turns behauptet.

## What platform is your computer?

Codex lief unter Linux/WSL2: `Linux 6.6.87.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2`. Die betroffene Anwendung wurde zusätzlich von einem MacBook über Tailscale genutzt.

## What terminal emulator and version are you using?

Lokale Codex-Sitzung mit Herdr als Multiplexer und separatem AGY-Implementierungsagenten. Die genaue Herdr-/Terminalversion ist für den historischen Lauf nicht gebunden.

## Codex doctor report

Nicht angehängt. Gemeldet wird eine Fehlleistung bei der langfristigen Zielsteuerung, kein lokaler Installationsfehler oder Crash. Version, Modellkonfiguration und Betriebssystem wurden für diese Meldung gezielt geprüft. Vollständige lokale Diagnostik, private Projektquellen und Sitzungsdaten werden nicht öffentlich eingestellt.

## What issue are you seeing?

**Codex verlor über mehr als zwölf Stunden den Bezug zum autorisierten Nutzerziel und ließ eine selbst eingeführte Analyse- und Diagnosekonstruktion immer weiter wachsen.** Trotz zahlreicher Reparaturrunden, Tests, Reviews und Receipts gab es am Ende keine integrierte Ladezeitreparatur und keinen gemessenen schnelleren tatsächlichen Kundenbericht.

Das Ziel war konkret: Ein vorhandener vollständiger dynamischer Bericht sollte über den bestehenden privaten Tailscale-Zugang schneller nutzbar werden. Beobachtet waren ungefähr 20 Sekunden bis zur Ladeanzeige und weitere 15 Sekunden bis zum vollständigen Bericht. Anmeldung, Daten, sieben vorhandene Angebotsinhalte, Sprache, Theme und direkte Abschnittslinks sollten erhalten bleiben.

Ich autorisierte Planung, Umsetzung durch AGY und Prüfung mit Nacharbeit bis zur verifizierten Reparatur. Codex sollte den Auftrag selbstständig führen und fremdes Dateieigentum sowie bestehende Sicherheitsgrenzen respektieren. Es sollte keine neuen Providerläufe, Workflows oder Datenbankmutationen starten.

Statt früh die tatsächlichen Ladephasen und die Machbarkeit der privaten Auslieferung zu belegen, wurden lokale Teilprüfungen zum Fortschrittsmaß. Der vorbereitete Buildweg erhielt eine eigene JavaScript-Semantikanalyse und anschließend einen eigenen privaten Diagnosetransport. Deren Randfälle führten zu immer weiteren Reparaturen. Ein externer, unabhängig geprüfter Snapshot umfasste 4.518 Buildzeilen und 8.183 Testzeilen; diese Zahlen beziehen sich auf einen bestimmten externen Stand, nicht auf aktive integrierte Produktdateien oder den neuesten unratifizierten Stand.

Codex unterbrach den Implementierungsagenten mehrfach früh. Ich musste mindestens 20 Minuten ungestörte Arbeitszeit verlangen. Codex verursachte außerdem einen frühen Fehler bei der Initialisierung eines privaten Zustands und musste eigene Aussagen über Tests und Ausführungsbelege später korrigieren.

Als ich nach mehr als zwölf Stunden fragte, ob Codex sich verrannt habe, bestätigte es verlorene Ergebnissteuerung bei zu viel Detailkontrolle. Ein von mir übermitteltes unabhängiges Red-Review bewertete auch das anschließende CTO-Memo mit **CHANGES REQUESTED**: Die Vorlage ließ einen Neuaufbau mit Standardmitteln aus, setzte Messung und Fernquellenprüfung erneut zu spät und erwähnte einen bereits dokumentierten Vollpollingbefund nicht. Eine Vertragsregel, welche die problematischen Chunkregeln festschrieb, war als Mitursache zu wenig berücksichtigt.

Der heutige lesend geprüfte Page-Stand enthält bereits Statusabrufe und Sessionzeitmarken. Der historische Pollingfehler wird deshalb nicht als unverändert aktueller Fehler oder als bewiesene Ursache der zusätzlichen 15 Sekunden ausgegeben. Der tatsächliche neue Ladezeitnachweis fehlt weiterhin.

**Auswirkung:** Mehr als zwölf Stunden nach meiner Nutzerbeobachtung, erhebliche zusätzliche Komplexität und Prüfverwaltung, kein erreichtes Produktziel, Vertrauensverlust und Kündigung meines Abos für 200 USD pro Monat.

## What steps can reproduce the bug?

Dies ist ein konkreter Langzeitvorfall aus einem privaten Projekt, **kein deterministischer öffentlicher Minimalreproducer**. Das Repo, vollständige Transkripte und Zugangsdaten sind nicht öffentlich. Die Abfolge war:

1. Codex mit `gpt-6.1-sol` und Reasoning `high` mit einer bestehenden Anwendung und einer messbaren Ladezeitbeschwerde beauftragen.
2. Einen vorhandenen Architekturvertrag auf Durchführbarkeit prüfen und einen Engineeringplan erstellen lassen.
3. Die Umsetzung über einen separaten Implementierungsagenten autorisieren. Die zentrale Vorgabe war: Implementierung überprüfen und den Agenten nacharbeiten lassen, bis die Probleme behoben sind.
4. Codex Analyse, Delegation und unabhängige Prüfung führen lassen; Produktcode und Integration bleiben beim Implementierungsagenten. Benutzeranweisungen, Skills und lokale Orchestrierung sind Teil dieses konkreten Setups.
5. Über viele serielle Reparaturrunden beobachten, dass die eigene Buildanalyse und Fehlerdiagnose wächst, während tatsächlicher Appbuild, Integration und Produktmessung ausbleiben.
6. Nach mehr als zwölf Stunden eine explizite Selbstprüfung und ein CTO-Memo verlangen. Codex räumt Zielverlust ein; ein unabhängiger Review findet weiterhin eine unvollständige Wegwahl und falsch angeordnete Machbarkeitsprüfungen.

Der ausführliche anonymisierte Fallbericht folgt unten. Die Meldung beweist nicht, dass der gleiche Verlauf in einer frischen Standardsitzung zwangsläufig reproduzierbar ist, oder dass allein das Modell statt des Zusammenspiels mit den Anweisungen und der Orchestrierung die Ursache war. Sie beschreibt die beobachtete Fehlleistung des Codex-Leitungspfads mit der genannten Modelleinstellung.

## What is the expected behavior?

- Das vollständige Nutzerziel über lange Arbeit erhalten und Fortschritt an tatsächlicher Integration und messbarer Wirkung beurteilen.
- Die billigsten aussagekräftigen Machbarkeits- und Engpassprüfungen vor weiteren Bauaufwand setzen: Phasen-Baseline am bestehenden Bericht und tatsächliche private Socket-Quellklasse.
- Eine blockierende Vertragsvorgabe ausdrücklich zur Prüfung stellen, statt fortgesetzt ihre nachgelagerten Symptome auszubauen.
- Nach mehreren Runden ohne Annäherung an das Ziel den Implementierungsweg hinterfragen und alle relevanten Alternativen vorlegen, einschließlich eines kleineren Neuaufbaus mit etablierten Werkzeugen.
- Dem Implementierungsagenten angemessene ungestörte Arbeitszeit lassen und eigene Fehlannahmen vermeiden beziehungsweise zügig korrigieren.
- Architekturfreigabe, historisches Teilreview, aktueller Gesamtstatus, integrierter Code und erreichtes Nutzerergebnis klar unterscheiden.
- Sicherheitsanforderungen und echte bestätigte Fehler weiter ernst nehmen. Eine Vereinfachung darf diese nicht still umgehen.
- Früh einen echten Blocker oder eine erforderliche Entscheidung verständlich vorlegen, statt erst nach einer vom Nutzer angestoßenen Selbstprüfung den Zielverlust zu erkennen.

## Additional information

Die zwölf Stunden sind meine Beobachtung als Nutzer, keine aus allen Prozesslaufzeiten berechnete Messung. Die Kündigung ist meine ausdrückliche Angabe als Abonnent. Interne Projekt-, Kunden-, Peer-, Pfad- und Sitzungskennungen sowie Zugangsdaten wurden weggelassen.

Diese Meldung unterscheidet eine frühere technische Trace-Reparatur von der anschließenden Ladeoptimierung des Kundenberichts. Sie behauptet weder, dass die gesamte Arbeit ohne jeden Teilerfolg war, noch, dass Codex ein nicht erreichtes Gesamtergebnis als fertig ausgegeben hätte. Der Kernfehler war die fortgesetzte, nicht zum Nutzerziel konvergierende Arbeit trotz wiederholt dokumentiertem offenen Gesamtstatus. Die spätere Selbstkorrektur musste ebenfalls unabhängig nachgebessert werden.
