# Feedback an OpenAI: Codex verlor bei einer langen Umsetzung das eigentliche Ziel

## Zusammenfassung

Ich beauftragte Codex, die Ladezeit eines bestehenden dynamischen Kundenberichts zu verbessern. Codex sollte die Umsetzung durch einen separaten Implementierungsagenten koordinieren, dessen Ergebnis selbst überprüfen und bestätigte Probleme bis zur geprüften Reparatur nacharbeiten lassen.

Nach meiner Beobachtung arbeitete Codex mehr als zwölf Stunden an diesem Vorgang. Es entstanden umfangreicher vorbereiteter Code, Tests, Reviews und Dokumentation. Das gewünschte Ergebnis war weiterhin nicht erreicht: Es gab keine integrierte Reparatur und keinen Nachweis, dass der tatsächliche Bericht schneller geladen wurde. Codex bestätigte diese Grenze bei einer anschließenden Selbstprüfung.

Die Arbeitszeit ist hier meine Beobachtung als Nutzer, keine nachträglich aus vollständig erfassten Laufzeiten berechnete Messung. Die übrige Darstellung beruht auf dem Gespräch, dem Arbeitsplan und den protokollierten Umsetzungs- und Reviewständen. Interne Zugangs-, Kunden- und Projektkennungen sind weggelassen.

## 1. Ausgangslage: Was sollte verbessert werden?

Ich nutzte eine bestehende Webanwendung über einen privaten Tailscale-Zugang auf meinem MacBook. Der vollständige Kundenbericht enthielt bereits dynamische Daten und die benötigten Inhalte. Das Problem war seine langsame Verfügbarkeit beim Fernzugriff.

Ich beobachtete ungefähr zwanzig Sekunden bis zur Anzeige, dass der Bericht geladen werde, und anschließend ungefähr weitere fünfzehn Sekunden bis zum vollständigen Bericht. Die insgesamt etwa fünfunddreißig Sekunden erschwerten die praktische Arbeit mit der Anwendung.

Eine frühere Diagnose reproduzierte bei simulierten 380 Millisekunden Verbindungslatenz und angenommenen 10 Mbit/s ungefähr zwanzig Sekunden bis zur Ladeanzeige und dreiundzwanzig Sekunden bis zum beobachteten Berichtsabschnitt. Sie erklärte also einen wesentlichen Teil des Problems, aber nicht die gesamten von mir beobachteten fünfunddreißig Sekunden. Insbesondere die zusätzliche Wartezeit auf Sitzung, Daten und vollständige Darstellung blieb zu untersuchen.

Die Unterhaltung hatte zuvor auch eine andere Oberfläche behandelt: die Lesbarkeit einer technischen Traceansicht. Die hier beschriebene lange Umsetzung betraf den anschließenden Auftrag zur Auslieferung des Kundenberichts. Diese beiden Flächen dürfen bei der Bewertung nicht vermischt werden.

## 2. Ziel und Bedeutung des Auftrags

Das Ziel war, den vorhandenen vollständigen Bericht über denselben privaten Zugang messbar schneller lesen zu können. Seine dynamischen Inhalte, bestehende URLs, Anmeldung, Sprache, Theme und direkte Abschnittslinks sollten erhalten bleiben. Ich präzisierte die Inhaltsprüfung auf die sieben vorhandenen Angebotsinhalte.

Weniger Dateien oder kleinere Downloads wären sinnvolle technische Mittel gewesen. Als Erfolg galt jedoch der tatsächlich schneller lesbare Bericht. Auch eine schnelle Ladeanzeige allein hätte das Ziel nicht erfüllt.

Das war wichtig, weil ich mit dem Bericht arbeiten wollte. Eine lange Wartezeit bis zu den Inhalten machte den vorgesehenen Fernzugriff unpraktisch. Ich wollte eine überprüfbare Verbesserung einer vorhandenen Anwendung, einschließlich ihrer bestehenden Funktionen.

## 3. Mein Auftrag an Codex

Ich bat zunächst darum, den vorhandenen Architekturvertrag auf Machbarkeit und verbleibende Arbeit zu prüfen und daraus einen konkreten Engineeringplan zu machen. Anschließend autorisierte ich die Umsetzung. Meine ausdrückliche Vorgabe lautete, dass Codex die Implementierung überprüfen und den Implementierungsagenten so lange nacharbeiten lassen sollte, bis die Probleme behoben seien.

Die Rollen waren klar: Der separate Agent sollte Produktcode, Integration und Tests bearbeiten. Codex sollte analysieren, koordinieren, Ergebnisse lesend überprüfen und die unabhängige Prüfung organisieren. Bestehende fremde Änderungen mussten geschützt werden. Neue Providerläufe, neue Workflows, Datenbankmutationen oder eine Ausweitung der Zugriffsrechte waren nicht Teil dieses Auftrags.

Ich erwartete, dass Codex die Arbeit selbstständig bis zum überprüften Ergebnis führt, notwendige Grenzen einhält und rechtzeitig erkennt, wenn der gewählte Lösungsweg nicht zum Ziel führt.

## 4. Der vorgesehene Lösungsansatz

Die Diagnose deutete darauf hin, dass der Browser über die Fernverbindung viele voneinander abhängige Entwicklungsdateien laden musste. Die Grundidee war deshalb, die Anwendung für diesen privaten Zugriff in wenige gebündelte und komprimierte Ressourcen zu übersetzen.

Der bestehende Server sollte weiterlaufen. Die gebündelte Oberfläche sollte dieselben dynamischen Daten und dieselbe Anmeldung verwenden. Sichere Konfiguration, unveränderliche Pakete und die Unterstützung bereits offener älterer Tabs gehörten zum akzeptierten Vertrag.

Der Plan sah zuerst einen isolierten Build und eine unveröffentlichte Messung am tatsächlichen Bericht vor. Anschließend sollten sichere Veröffentlichung, Integration und Fernabnahme folgen. Ein positives Architekturreview bestätigte diesen Zielvertrag. Es bewies noch keine Implementierung oder Ladezeitwirkung.

## 5. Ab wann und weshalb ging die Arbeit schief?

Der erste konkrete vermeidbare Fehler trat früh auf: Codex ließ einen noch ungeprüften Initialisierungsbaustein einen tatsächlichen privaten Zustand vorbereiten. Die dabei erzeugte falsche Bindung wurde zu einem zusätzlichen Betriebsblocker. Codex hielt später selbst fest, dass dieser Schritt bis zur geprüften Initialisierung hätte zurückgehalten werden müssen.

Der grundlegende Verlust der Zielsteuerung wurde während der wiederholten Nacharbeiten an Messwerkzeug und Build deutlich. Codex bearbeitete gefundene Fehler in immer kleineren seriellen Einheiten. Nach jedem korrigierten Teil folgten ein neuer Auftrag, Tests, eingefrorene Quellen, Quittungen und weitere Reviews. Viele einzelne Fehler wurden behoben. Ein tatsächlicher Clientkandidat und der neue Ladezeitvergleich blieben weiterhin unerreicht.

Der Buildweg entwickelte sich dabei zu einer umfangreichen eigenen Analyse von JavaScript. Er sollte Variablenbindungen, dynamische und optionale Konfigurationszugriffe, Transformationen und verschiedene erzeugte Programme beurteilen. Diese Eigenkonstruktion brachte weitere Randfälle und Fehlklassifikationen hervor. Im letzten unabhängig geprüften Stand umfasste der Buildbaustein 4.518 Dateizeilen und seine Testdatei 8.183 Zeilen. Das sind Größenangaben einschließlich eingebetteter Programme, Kommentare und Tests, keine genaue Zählung produktiver Logik.

Ein weiteres Abbiegen entstand durch die Diagnose des ersten abgelehnten Bibliothekszugriffs. Diese Beobachtung erhielt eine eigene Quellaufnahme, Zuordnung von Textstellen und einen privaten Dateitransport. Anschließend beschäftigten die Arbeit die Sicherheit und Korrektheit dieser Diagnose: Dateiidentität, Schreibrechte, Bereinigung, Aufbewahrung und tatsächliche Testpfade. Die Diagnose wurde damit selbst zu einem zusätzlichen umfangreichen System vor der eigentlichen Ladezeitmessung.

Ein konkreter Quellenbefund zeigte außerdem, dass die gewählte Chunkkonfiguration schon einer minimalen Testanwendung zusätzliche Bibliothekswurzeln aufzwang. Der eigene vorgelagerte Validator lehnte einen Zugriff ab, bevor die normale Vite-Transformation wirken konnte. Codex hätte die Notwendigkeit und tatsächliche Wirkung dieses Bauwegs früher untersuchen müssen. Stattdessen floss weitere Zeit in die Absicherung der Fehlerbeobachtung.

Der akzeptierte Architekturvertrag schrieb gerade diese bestehenden Chunkregeln fest. Der Blocker war daher auch durch eine konkrete Vertragsvorgabe mitverursacht. Codex hätte diesen Zusammenhang als Grund für eine ausdrückliche Vertragsprüfung behandeln müssen. Stattdessen konzentrierte es die Reparatur auf den nachgelagerten eigenen Analyse- und Diagnoseapparat.

## 6. Welche Fehler machte Codex als Leitung?

**Codex bewertete Fortschritt zu stark anhand abgeschlossener Teilprüfungen.** Grüne Tests und positive eng begrenzte Reviews wurden zum Anlass für die nächste Nacharbeit. Zu wenig wirksam war die Frage, was diese Runde zum funktionierenden tatsächlichen Bericht beitrug.

**Codex hinterfragte die gewählte Implementierungsform zu spät.** Die Architekturprüfung wurde zu stark als Bestätigung des konkreten Bauwegs behandelt. Dass ein Zielvertrag sinnvoll ist, bedeutet jedoch nicht, dass jede zu seiner Umsetzung entstandene Eigenkonstruktion erforderlich oder angemessen ist.

**Codex unterbrach den Implementierungsagenten mehrfach zu früh.** Wiederholte Recherche oder ein noch fehlender Edit führten zu Stopps und weiterer Zerlegung. Ich musste ausdrücklich verlangen, mindestens zwanzig Minuten ungestörte Arbeitszeit zu gewähren. Danach wurde diese Vorgabe eingehalten. Die zusätzliche Geduld behob jedoch nicht den bereits aufgeblähten Aufgabenweg.

**Codex verursachte zusätzliche Nacharbeit durch eigene Fehler.** Dazu gehörten der frühe Initialisierungsschritt und falsche Annahmen über Transformationen beziehungsweise Ausführungsbelege. Später mussten auch Angaben über ausgeführte Tests, zeitliche Quellenstände und tatsächliche Prozessexits präzisiert werden.

**Codex erzeugte viel Verwaltungsarbeit und leitete zu spät Konsequenzen daraus ab.** Quellbindungen, Quittungen und unabhängige Reviews sind teilweise erforderlich. Hier entstand aber ein erheblicher eigener Arbeitsstrom zur Verwaltung zahlreicher Zwischenstände. Codex dokumentierte wiederholt, dass das Gesamtziel nicht erreicht sei, ohne den Bauweg entsprechend früh neu zu bewerten.

## 7. Was war tatsächlich erreicht?

Es gab vorbereitete Komponenten für Messung, Initialisierung und Build sowie nachweislich reparierte Fehler. Mehrere Teilstände bestanden gezielte Tests und erhielten begrenzte positive Reviews. Die Arbeit war daher nicht vollständig ergebnislos.

Die Produktwirkung fehlte jedoch weiterhin. Die sieben vorgesehenen Kandidatendateien lagen im externen Staging und waren noch nicht in die aktive Anwendung integriert. Es gab keinen nachgewiesen erfolgreichen vollständigen neuen Appbuild, keinen neuen Ladezeitvergleich des tatsächlich ausgelieferten Berichts und keine abschließende Fernabnahme auf dem MacBook.

Die jüngste Lieferung des Implementierungsagenten meldete erneut erfolgreiche gezielte Tests und einen engen Compilercheck. Ihre unabhängige Abnahme stand noch aus. Ein solcher Teilstand darf weder als vollständige technische Fertigstellung noch als erfüllter Nutzerauftrag dargestellt werden.

## 8. Was die unabhängige Kritik am eigenen CTO-Memo zusätzlich zeigte

Als ich schließlich eine kritische Bestandsaufnahme verlangte, räumte Codex seine verlorene Zielsteuerung ein und schrieb ein CTO-Memo. Ein anschließend von mir übermitteltes unabhängiges Red-Review bewertete aber auch dieses Memo mit „CHANGES REQUESTED“, also mit der Forderung nach Nachbesserung. Es bestätigte wesentliche Teile der Diagnose, fand jedoch weitere Fehler in der Entscheidungsvorlage.

**Die vorgeschlagene Wahl war unvollständig.** Codex stellte die Vereinfachung des Eigenbaus seinem vollständigen Weiterbau gegenüber. Damit setzte es in beiden Wegen den vorhandenen umfangreichen Code als Ausgangspunkt voraus. Ein schlanker Neuaufbau mit etablierten Vite-Mitteln fehlte als dritte Option: normale Konfiguration und Ersetzungen, eine andere Form der Chunkzuordnung sowie bestehende statische Auslieferung und Vorkompression. Ob diese Option alle Anforderungen erfüllt, müsste geprüft werden. Schon investierte Arbeit rechtfertigt aber nicht, sie aus der Wahl auszuschließen.

**Die Reihenfolge der nächsten Schritte war weiterhin falsch.** Das Memo wollte zunächst einen neuen Kandidaten bauen und danach messen. Dabei enthielt der bestehende Plan bereits einen bestätigten Codebefund: Die Seite hatte bei laufender Statusprüfung wiederholt den vollständigen Bericht mit historisch ungefähr 743 kB geladen, obwohl ein schmaler Statusabruf verfügbar war. Auf der langsamen Fernstrecke war das eine konkrete Hypothese für zusätzliche Wartezeit. Codex ließ diesen Befund im ersten Memo aus. Er gehört zum bestehenden Auftrag eines anderen Dateieigentümers; seine Existenz hätte dennoch meine Entscheidung informieren müssen.

Bei der heutigen lesenden Nachprüfung enthält die Seite bereits Statusabrufe und Zeitmarken. Der historische Fehler darf deshalb nicht als ungeprüfte Behauptung über den heutigen Zustand fortgeschrieben werden. Ebenso ist bisher nicht bewiesen, dass er die zusätzlichen fünfzehn Sekunden verursachte. Gerade deshalb braucht es zuerst eine aktuelle Phasenmessung am bestehenden Bericht, die Sitzung, Transfer, Datenverarbeitung und Darstellung unterscheidet.

**Eine tragende Machbarkeitsfrage kam zu spät.** Der Architekturvertrag wählt die gebündelte Auslieferung anhand der tatsächlichen Fernquelle am bestehenden Server. Kommt der Zugriff aufgrund der Weiterleitung dort wie ein lokaler Zugriff an, funktioniert dieser Auswahlmechanismus für meinen Zugang nicht. Codex nannte die offene Frage, stellte die Prüfung jedoch erst hinter den Bauaufwand. Eine Beobachtung der tatsächlichen Socket-Quellklasse beim echten Fernaufruf gehört an den Anfang.

**Auch der Entscheidungsstand war nicht ausreichend greifbar.** Der aktuelle umfangreiche Eigenbau lag außerhalb des aktiven Repos. Die Zahlen 4.518 und 8.183 beziehen sich auf hashgebundene externe Dateien eines bestimmten Reviewstands. Im Repo lagen ältere, kleinere Reviewkopien. Es gab keinen aktuellen geprüften Gesamtstatus. Vor einer informierten Wahl braucht es einen benennbaren aktuellen Reviewstand, die vollständige relevante Testsuite und einen passenden frischen Compilercheck mit gesicherten Prozessexits. Eine Tabelle vieler historischer Teilerfolge ersetzt diesen Bestandsnachweis nicht.

Das Red-Review verlangte außerdem eine verständliche Erklärung des frühen Initialisierungsfehlers. Seine praktische Folge ist, dass der falsch gebundene private Zustand nicht als zulässiger Veröffentlichungszustand verwendet werden kann. Die Auswahl ist deaktiviert; ein stilles Zurücksetzen würde die Zuordnung und Fehlerhistorie verändern. Ein tatsächlicher Datenverlust oder eine Veröffentlichung privater Daten ist damit nicht belegt.

Damit zeigte sich das Problem auch in Codex' Selbstkorrektur: Es erkannte den verlorenen Fokus, bereitete aber zunächst erneut eine verengte Wegwahl mit verspäteten Machbarkeitsprüfungen vor. Das Memo ist inzwischen entsprechend überarbeitet. Diese Überarbeitung ist noch nicht unabhängig ratifiziert und ersetzt weiterhin keine Produktreparatur.

## 9. Was hätte ich von Codex erwartet?

Codex hätte die tragenden Fragen früher prüfen müssen: Lässt sich der tatsächlich benötigte Client sicher bauen? Kann der bestehende Server meinen privaten Fernzugriff zuverlässig erkennen? Verbessert das Bundle die Zeit bis zum vollständigen Bericht, und wo verbleibt gegebenenfalls die zusätzliche Wartezeit?

Nach mehreren Reparaturrunden ohne Annäherung an diese Nachweise hätte Codex den Bauweg selbstständig kritisch bewerten müssen. Eine unnötige fehlerhafte Eigenkonstruktion sauber zu entfernen oder zu vereinfachen ist ebenfalls eine Lösung. Bestätigte Fehler dürfen dabei nicht ignoriert, Sicherheitsanforderungen nicht geschwächt und notwendige Architekturentscheidungen nicht still getroffen werden.

Ich erwarte weder ungeprüfte Schnellschüsse noch das Überspringen von Reviews. Ich erwarte, dass Codex zwischen dem vollständigen Nutzerziel, zwingenden Voraussetzungen und selbst eingeführter zusätzlicher Komplexität unterscheidet und daraus wirksame nächste Schritte ableitet.

## 10. Warum ich diesen Fall an OpenAI weitergeben möchte

Der Fall zeigt ein Problem bei langer autonomer Arbeit: Codex kann über viele Runden sorgfältig lesen, delegieren, testen und dokumentieren, während der eigentliche Auftrag weiterhin unerfüllt bleibt. Lokale Verfahrensqualität genügt offenbar nicht, um die globale Zielsteuerung zu erhalten.

Aus meiner Sicht sollte Codex besser erkennen, wenn Reparaturschleifen nicht zum Ergebnis konvergieren, zusätzliche Diagnose mehr Aufwand erzeugt als sie Nutzen liefert oder ein Implementierungsweg immer neue Sonderprobleme hervorbringt. Dann sollte es den einfacheren verantwortbaren Weg zum gleichen vollständigen Ziel vorbereiten und eine tatsächlich erforderliche Entscheidung rechtzeitig verständlich vorlegen.

Besonders wichtig wären eine frühere Prüfung der tatsächlichen Produktwirkung, angemessene ungestörte Delegationszeit und eine klare Trennung zwischen Architekturfreigabe, Teilreview, integriertem Code und erreichtem Nutzerergebnis.

Der Fall zeigt zusätzlich, dass ein Agent auch seine eigene nachträgliche Diagnose nicht allein bestätigen sollte. Vertragsvorgaben können Fehlwege mitverursachen; ein scheinbar vollständiger Plan kann die entscheidenden Alternativen auslassen. Eine robuste Selbstkorrektur muss deshalb die Voraussetzungen des bisherigen Wegs und die Reihenfolge der billigsten aussagekräftigen Prüfungen hinterfragen.

Der Nutzer musste hier nach mehr als zwölf Stunden selbst fragen, ob Codex sich verrannt habe. Codex bestätigte anschließend verlorene Ergebnissteuerung bei zu viel Detailkontrolle. Diese Neubewertung hätte wesentlich früher aus der Leitung des Agenten selbst kommen müssen.

</details>

### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

Installed Windows package: `OpenAI.Codex 26.930.2377.0` (queried via Get-AppxPackage; About dialog not inspected).

### What subscription do you have?

Not collected; this report concerns local browser discovery and native-host provisioning.

### What platform is your computer?

Windows x64, OS version `10.0.26300`, build `26300`.

### What issue are you seeing?

The official ChatGPT extension is installed and enabled in Google Chrome Dev, but it cannot connect to the running Codex/ChatGPT desktop app. Read-only diagnostics show a channel/profile detection mismatch and missing native messaging registration.

Environment:
- Running browser: `C:\Program Files\Google\Chrome Dev\Application\chrome.exe`
- Chrome Dev version: `156.0.8072.0`
- ChatGPT extension ID: `hehggadaopoacecdllhhajmbjkdcmajg`
- Extension version: `1.26.901.11451`
- Active profile: `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Google\Chrome Dev\User Data\Default`

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Using the bundled `app/resources/plugins/openai-bundled/plugins/chrome/scripts` diagnostics:

1. Run `node check-extension-installed.js --browser chrome --json` without an override.
   - It checks `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Google\Chrome\User Data`.
   - Result: `installed: false`, `enabled: false`, exit code 2.
2. Set `CODEX_CHROMIUM_USER_DATA_DIR` to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Google\Chrome Dev\User Data` and run the same check.
   - Result: `installed: true`, `registered: true`, `enabled: true`, `disabled: false`, `disableReasons: []`, exit code 0.
   - Selected profile: `Default`; extension version `1.26.901.11451_0`.
3. Run `node installed-browsers.js --json`.
   - It includes the actual Chrome Dev executable but labels it generically as Google Chrome.
   - The default HTTP/HTTPS ProgID is `ChromeDHTML`.
   - It also lists another Chrome executable; this is not a claim that Chrome Dev is the only installed browser.
4. Run `node check-native-host-manifest.js --browser chrome --json`.
   - `registryManifestPath: null`, `exists: false`, `correct: false`.
   - Reported missing key: `HKCU\Software\Google\Chrome\NativeMessagingHosts\com.openai.codexextension`.
   - Reported missing manifest: `%LOCALAPPDATA%\OpenAI\extension\com.openai.codexextension.json`.
5. Both `%LOCALAPPDATA%\OpenAI\Codex\chrome-native-hosts-v2.json` and `%USERPROFILE%\.codex\chrome-native-hosts-v2.json` are absent.
6. Browser inventory in this Codex chat contains only the in-app browser and MCP Apps, with no connected Chrome extension browser.

### What is the expected behavior?

The app should discover the installed and enabled ChatGPT extension in the selected/running Chrome Dev profile. It should provision and verify a usable native-host connection through its supported setup flow, or clearly explain that the Chrome release channel is unsupported / setup is incomplete.

Default diagnostics should not report the extension missing solely because they inspected the stable-Chrome profile directory while the extension is present in Chrome Dev.

### Additional information

Related reports:
- #40414 describes a similar Chrome Dev channel/profile detection gap on macOS. This report supplies Windows-specific evidence.
- #42520 describes missing Windows v2 registration with native messaging already installed. Here the basic native messaging key and manifest are also missing.
- #47874 describes a Windows connection failure with existing native-host registration, unlike the observed state here.

The profile detection mismatch is confirmed by the two diagnostic runs. The reason native-host provisioning did not occur is not established, and no claim is made that the profile mismatch alone caused it. No reinstall was attempted or verified, and no native-host manifest, registry entry, app code, browser profile, or security setting was modified during this investigation. The bundled Chrome troubleshooting guidance advises against manually repairing the native host, so investigation stopped at read-only evidence rather than applying an unsupported workaround.

## Problem

After the last two desktop app updates, ordinary interactions repeatedly caused severe freezes and Windows “Not responding”: opening or reactivating a window, switching conversations, opening Settings, and typing. This seriously disrupted normal use.

## Local recovery

Local troubleshooting identified a missing bundled runtime cache matching the installed app. The app repeatedly attempted synchronous runtime preparation and failed, blocking the interface.

The matching runtime was copied from the currently installed official application package into its expected cache location, and the copied files were verified against the originals. The application installation, conversations, authentication, and security settings were preserved; the app did not need to be restarted.

After this repair, window interaction checks no longer showed the original unresponsive behavior. The user confirmed that use is temporarily normal again, but is unsure whether the problem will recur.

## Requested fix

Please investigate runtime cache deployment after updates and prevent repeated synchronous preparation failures from blocking normal UI interaction. The exact underlying cause of the preparation failure has not been established. The local repair restores the current runtime cache and is not evidence of a permanent fix for future updates.

This submission contains only a description of the problem and the recovery method. No diagnostic report, logs, attachments, local paths, account details, or conversation contents are included.

### What version of the Codex App are you using (From "About Codex" dialog)?

26.930.2377.0 (installed via Microsoft Store). Cannot actually reach the "About" dialog since the app is blocked before any UI loads — version confirmed via `Get-AppxPackage` / Windows AppX deployment event log instead.

### What subscription do you have?

Personal workspace (ChatGPT Plus/Free tier) — **not** a Business/Enterprise/Edu managed workspace. This is notable because the failure is in a code path that fetches "organization"/workspace network policy, which I'd expect to only apply to managed workspaces.

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26300.0 x64 (Windows 11 Pro)

### What issue are you seeing?

Every time the app launches, it immediately shows a blocking error dialog and never reaches the chat UI:

- Title (i18n key `desktop.workspacePolicyRecovery.title`): "Organization settings could not be loaded"
- Detail (i18n key `desktop.workspacePolicyRecovery.detail`): "The app is paused until your organization settings can be loaded safely. A network connection, proxy, or firewall may be blocking access. Check your connection and try again, or sign out to use another account. If the problem continues, contact your IT administrator."

Only options are Retry / Sign out / Quit, and none of them resolve it — Retry just shows the same dialog again.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Have the Codex Windows desktop app auto-update via Microsoft Store from 26.928.4866.0 to 26.930.2377.0.
2. Launch the app (sign-in uses ChatGPT account / browser sign-in with Google SSO, not an API key).
3. The error dialog above appears immediately, every time, with no way to get past it.

Confirmed via Windows AppX deployment event log that the auto-update to 26.930.2377.0 happened at 2026-10-02 16:04:46 KST (UTC+9), and the app has been broken on every launch since that exact moment. It worked fine on 26.928.4866.0 immediately before that.

Troubleshooting already done to rule out local/network causes:
- Logging into chatgpt.com in a regular browser on the same machine/account works perfectly and shows account/workspace data correctly.
- Verified TLS/network connectivity from this machine to chatgpt.com and api.openai.com (valid cert chain, no proxy, no MITM). `wss://chatgpt.com/` WebSocket handshake gets a clean HTTP 403 from the server (not a dropped/reset connection), so WebSocket traffic is not being blocked either.
- Fully uninstalled and reinstalled the Codex app (wipes all local app data/profile/cookies) — identical error persists.
- Restarted the `CodexSandboxService.OpenAI.Codex` Windows service — no change.
- Removed local third-party security software — no change.

By inspecting `app.asar`, I traced the error to this logic (paraphrased from the minified bundle), which parses an "application network requirements" (workspace policy) response from the backend:

```
if (parsed.requirements.application === undefined && !(serverVersion != null && isAtLeast(serverVersion, "0.141.0") && isLessThan(serverVersion, CURRENT_APP_VERSION)))
  throw Error("This app server did not provide application network requirements.")
```

and a schema-validation failure path that throws:

```
"Application network requirements are invalid or unavailable. Update the app server to a version that exposes application requirements."
```

This points to a compatibility gap between the 26.930.2377.0 client's expectations for the workspace/org network-policy response and what the backend is actually returning — and since this is happening on a **personal** (non-managed) workspace, it looks like the new build may be mishandling the "no organization policy configured" case (which should presumably just resolve to `{kind: "unrestricted"}`) as a hard failure instead.

### What is the expected behavior?

The app should load normally. For a personal (non-managed) workspace in particular, there shouldn't be any "organization network requirements" to fetch/enforce at all, so this code path should resolve to unrestricted/no-op rather than blocking the entire app.

### Additional information

- This looks like a staged/gradual-rollout regression: other devices on the same account that have not yet received the 26.930.2377.0 update are still on 26.928.4866.0 and work fine.
- Workaround in use: Codex via the web (chatgpt.com) while the desktop app is broken.
- Happy to provide further logs/diagnostics (e.g. `codex doctor` output from the CLI, network captures) if useful — just let me know what would help.

items.body:
## Summary

In the unified ChatGPT desktop app, existing **ChatGPT Spaces are visible in the sidebar**, but a normal Chat appears unable to discover or access those Spaces.

I can use normal Chat to access the general Library/files surface, including listing folders, reading files, searching content, and updating Library files. However, the Spaces shown in the sidebar are not exposed through that same hierarchy, and the Chat has no apparent way to enumerate or select an existing Space.

This prevents a normal Chat from using Spaces as a persistent knowledge workspace across conversations.

## Environment

- ChatGPT subscription: Pro
- Platform: macOS, Apple Silicon
- Desktop app: 26.930.21537
- Observed: October 2, 2026

## What I observed

The sidebar contains multiple existing Spaces.

From a normal Chat, the available file/Library capabilities successfully support:

- listing Library folders/files
- semantic file search
- reading files
- creating/updating/moving/deleting Library files and folders

But the normal Chat cannot discover the actual Spaces shown in the sidebar.

A concrete control test:

1. List the Library root and request only folders.
2. The result contains ordinary Library folders (for example, Google Drive and a normal user-created folder).
3. The Spaces visible in the desktop sidebar are **not** returned as folders or other objects.
4. Search the Library for content/names associated with those Spaces.
5. Results come from ordinary Library files; Space membership/context is not exposed.
6. Update a Markdown file in a normal Library folder.
7. The update succeeds, confirming that general Library access itself is working.

So this does not look like a blanket file-access failure. It looks like a boundary between **Library/files** and the actual **Space object/context**.

## Steps to reproduce

1. In ChatGPT desktop, create or open multiple Spaces so they are visible in the left sidebar.
2. Start a normal Chat outside a Space.
3. Ask ChatGPT to list the existing Spaces, open one by name, inspect its Pages, or update the most relevant Page inside it.
4. Observe that normal Chat can work with general Library/files, but cannot enumerate/select the existing Spaces.
5. Compare the sidebar with the Library root: the Spaces are visible in the UI but absent from the normal Chat's accessible hierarchy.

## Actual behavior

Normal Chat can operate on Library/files but has no apparent Space discovery/selection capability.

In the tested Chat surface, there is no equivalent of:

- list existing Spaces
- resolve a Space by name/ID
- list Pages belonging to a selected Space
- read/update a Page specifically within that Space

The result is that Chat can maintain ordinary Library files, but cannot reliably maintain the user's existing Space structure.

## Expected behavior

A normal Chat should be able to explicitly discover an existing Space and, when the user asks, read or update Pages inside it.

A useful flow would be:

1. User says, for example, "Update the relevant information in my existing Space."
2. Chat discovers the user's Spaces.
3. Chat selects the appropriate Space.
4. Chat inspects the existing Pages.
5. Chat updates the most relevant existing Page rather than creating an unrelated Library file.

This seems consistent with the documented product model where users can ask ChatGPT to create a Space and create/update Pages in a Space.

## Why this matters

Spaces are most useful as persistent, structured knowledge stores. If only the Chat opened from inside a specific Space can see that Space, while a normal Chat cannot discover existing Spaces, then cross-conversation maintenance is difficult.

For example, a user cannot naturally ask a normal Chat to:

- locate the appropriate existing Space,
- inspect the Pages already there,
- merge new decisions/status into the right Page,
- keep the Space current over time.

Instead, the information risks being written into unrelated Library files/folders.

I searched for duplicates before filing this. These appear related but not identical:

- #33723 — normal Chat loses cloud Project context when switching from Work/Codex
- #50205 — Space/Library Markdown URI is not resolved in Codex Local
- #49650 — Space/Page workflow where a Page is readable/writable but an automation attachment fails
- #49870 — Space setup failure in the macOS desktop app

This report is specifically about **normal Chat being unable to discover/access existing ChatGPT Spaces that are already visible in the UI**.

## Additional note

Issue #49650 indicates that Page-specific capabilities such as reading a Page exist in at least some Space/Dot contexts. That makes me wonder whether this is a tool-routing/context-exposure gap specific to normal Chat rather than a missing backend capability.

I can provide a screenshot showing the existing Spaces in the sidebar if useful.

items.title: Codex Cloud: S3 SigV4 requests fail with an empty signed Content-Length in the server canonical request

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: codex-web
labels.description: Issues related to Codex Web

labels.description: Issues involving networking or endpoint connectivity problems (disconnections)

items.body:
## Problem

In a Codex Cloud environment using the managed HTTP/HTTPS proxy, AWS SDK S3 `PutObject` requests fail with `403 SignatureDoesNotMatch`. This blocks `sst dev` when SST writes its stage lock/state.

A controlled diagnostic explicitly signed a nonempty `Content-Length`, but S3's error response showed an empty value for that header in its `CanonicalRequest`. This is consistent with a signed header being removed or changed along the request path. We have not isolated the exact proxy component responsible.

The AWS CLI successfully uploaded a disposable object through the same environment and cleaned it up. AWS authentication had succeeded before these probes; this is separate from an earlier expired-credential problem.

## Environment

- Codex Cloud Linux workspace; managed proxy configured through `HTTP_PROXY` and `HTTPS_PROXY` (`http://proxy:8080`).
- Node.js `v24.19.0`.
- Workspace JavaScript packages: `@aws-sdk/client-s3 3.1065.0`, `@smithy/node-http-handler 4.4.7`.
- SST `4.17.0`; its source declares AWS SDK Go v2 `1.36.2` and S3 module `1.53.1`.
- AWS region: `us-east-1`.

These observations come from the existing debugging session on October 2, 2026. Filing this issue did not rerun cloud writes or deployments.

## Reproduction / diagnostic procedure

1. In a Codex Cloud environment with the S3 destination allowed, configure valid AWS credentials and the environment proxy/CA for the client.
2. Compare an AWS CLI `s3api put-object` against an SDK `PutObject`, using a disposable diagnostic key and a small JSON body. Do not use a real SST state/lock key.
3. For a controlled signing comparison, construct a PUT request containing `content-length: String(Buffer.byteLength(body))`, sign it with the SDK's SigV4 signer, and send it through the SDK request handler. Confirm that `content-length` appears in `SignedHeaders`.
4. If S3 returns `SignatureDoesNotMatch`, compare only the `content-length` line in the returned `CanonicalRequest` with the outgoing value. Avoid publishing authorization headers, session tokens, or full canonical requests.

Recorded diagnostic results:

```text
CLI PutObject: PASS
CLI probe cleanup: PASS
JavaScript SDK PutObject failed: SignatureDoesNotMatch
Go-style headers, signing Content-Length=true: 403 SignatureDoesNotMatch
Server canonical Content-Length: [empty]
Explicit payload hash + signed Content-Length: 403 SignatureDoesNotMatch
Server canonical Content-Length: [empty]
JavaScript SDK explicit CONNECT: SignatureDoesNotMatch
```

Not signing `Content-Length` in one probe produced `501 NotImplemented`, so that did not establish a working fix.

## Expected behavior

Valid SigV4 requests should reach AWS without signed header values or payload semantics being changed. A nonempty signed `Content-Length` should not become empty in the server's canonical request.

## Attempts and impact

- Disabling optional request checksums did not fix startup.
- Forcing Go HTTP/1.1 did not fix it.
- An explicit JavaScript CONNECT proxy agent did not fix it.
- Supplying an explicit payload hash did not fix the signed-header diagnostic.
- Temporarily delegating SST state writes to the working AWS CLI got past the S3 failure, but is a local workaround rather than a general fix.

## Related guidance / request

An [AWS SDK maintainer explains](https://github.com/aws/aws-sdk-go-v2/issues/2722#issuecomment-2245813194) that proxies which add or remove signed headers can cause signature mismatches and must preserve the request. That upstream report concerns `Range`; this report concerns `Content-Length`.

Please investigate whether Codex Cloud's managed proxy strips or rewrites signed `Content-Length` values, including framing changes between client and upstream connections. If this transport is intentionally unsupported, please document the limitation and a supported way to use AWS SDKs/SST from Cloud.

Source inspection suggests this extends beyond cat:
- bat, batcat, less, and more also require a single file operand to produce a read action.
- head and tail with supported -n arguments, as well as supported sed and awk forms, extract only the first input file and omit subsequent files.

The cat behavior is backed by runtime observations and a local parser regression test. The additional commands listed above have been inspected in source but have not yet been individually reproduced at runtime.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Create two small files in the working directory used by a Codex app-server session:

   ```sh
   printf 'alpha\n' > A.md
   printf 'beta\n' > B.md
   ```

2. Ask Codex to execute these as two separate shell-tool calls, preserving the commands exactly:

   ```sh
   cat A.md
   ```

   ```sh
   cat A.md B.md
   ```

3. Capture the app-server `item/completed` notifications for the corresponding `commandExecution` items and inspect `commandActions`.

4. Compare the results:
   - `cat A.md` is classified as a `read` action for A.md.
   - `cat A.md B.md` is classified as `unknown`, with no `read` actions for either file.
   - The second command still exits successfully and outputs both `alpha` and `beta`.

The same classification issue can be reproduced directly in the shell-command parser by comparing:

- `parse_command(&["cat".into(), "A.md".into()])`
- `parse_command(&["cat".into(), "A.md".into(), "B.md".into()])`

The first returns a `ParsedCommand::Read`; the second returns a `ParsedCommand::Unknown`.

The relevant implementation is in `codex-rs/shell-command/src/parse_command.rs`: the `cat` branch calls `single_non_flag_operand`, which returns `None` when there is more than one file operand.

### What is the expected behavior?

For straightforward commands that read multiple explicitly named files, commandActions should include a separate read action for each file operand.

For example, `cat A.md B.md` should produce:
- A read action with path A.md.
- A read action with path B.md.

It should not classify the entire command as unknown solely because it has multiple file operands, or report only the first file while omitting subsequent files.

Single-file reads should retain their existing behavior. Complex or ambiguous shell expressions can remain conservatively classified as unknown; this report concerns simple commands with explicit file paths.

### Additional information

Relevant source:
https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/14a477ea89712071944244022e8a10142845456e/codex-rs/shell-command/src/parse_command.rs

For cat, the parser calls single_non_flag_operand(), which explicitly returns None when it encounters a second file operand. The caller then falls back to ParsedCommand::Unknown.

The bat/batcat, less, and more branches use the same helper. Other read branches, including supported head/tail, sed, and awk forms, select only the first file operand.

We discovered this in an integration using a downstream Codex build, then confirmed that the relevant logic is also present in the upstream source at the commit linked above. The cat behavior was reproduced in a local parser test; the other command variants are source-level findings.

We understand that commandActions is a command summary rather than a complete filesystem audit trail. This report concerns simple, explicit multi-file reads that the parser could represent without resolving dynamic shell expressions.

The requested outcome is complete representation of the explicit file paths. Separate read entries are one possible approach, but we are not prescribing a particular schema or implementation.

### What version of the Codex App are you using?

26.928.40906, build 12694, read from the installed macOS application's Info.plist.

### What subscription do you have?

Not included. The evidence below concerns the desktop plugin installation/authentication lifecycle.

### What platform is your computer?

macOS 27.0.1, arm64.

### What issue are you seeing?

The marketplace Cloudflare plugin installs successfully, completes MCP OAuth, and exposes working tools. It is then automatically uninstalled approximately 10 minutes after the installation OAuth pending record was created. Reinstalling and completing OAuth reproduces the same removal.

This happened twice during real use on 2026-10-02. Between installation and removal, authenticated Cloudflare API requests succeeded, including creation of a DNS record. After removal, the direct Cloudflare MCP tools disappeared. The app-wrapper fallback reported USER_NOT_LOGGED_IN for the plugin's required app connection.

No user uninstall action or agent invocation of a plugin-uninstall tool occurred at either removal. Desktop logs show the frontend-originated plugin/uninstall request and plugin_uninstall_succeeded.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Observed workflow:

1. Install Cloudflare 1.0.1 from openai-curated-remote using the desktop UI.
2. Complete the Cloudflare MCP OAuth flow.
3. Use the exposed Cloudflare MCP tools successfully.
4. Leave the desktop app running for about 10 minutes after installation begins.
5. Observe the plugin disappear and the direct MCP tools become unavailable.
6. Reinstall through the same UI, complete MCP OAuth, and observe the same delayed removal.

The necessary precondition appears to be that the required app connection remains unconnected even though the separate MCP connection has authenticated. I cannot yet specify what causes that app connection state mismatch, so these steps should not be read as guaranteeing reproduction for every account.

### Current evidence

All timestamps below are UTC, from desktop logs:

| Event | First occurrence | Second occurrence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| App connect OAuth pending state registered, resumeTarget=plugin-install | 07:55:33.155 | 08:14:49.718 |
| plugin_install_succeeded | 07:55:37.214 | 08:14:54.078 |
| MCP server OAuth login completed, name=cloudflare | 07:55:53.283 | 08:15:10.779 |
| app/installed response, errorCode=null | 08:05:35.682, durationMs=2518 | 08:24:51.959, durationMs=2235 |
| plugin/uninstall response | 08:05:37.152 | 08:24:53.412 |
| plugin_uninstall_succeeded | 08:05:37.152 | 08:24:53.413 |

Subtracting the app/installed request durations places those checks at almost exactly 600 seconds after each pending record was registered. The raw app/installed response payload was not captured; its callable=false outcome is inferred from the rollback branch, supported separately by the wrapper's USER_NOT_LOGGED_IN response.

Cloudflare plugin metadata declares both:

- mcp.json: cloudflare -> https://mcp.cloudflare.com/mcp
- .app.json: required=true for asdk_app_6abc2a9552748191b465859a06e90da3

The marketplace plugin identity is app-6a99ceead2c481919fb44845267235c4@openai-curated-remote. The desktop installation logs use plugin_asdk_app_6abc2a9552748191b465859a06e90da3.

### Client-side analysis

Read-only inspection of the installed renderer asset webview/assets/app-initial-27bc4044d9e8.js found:

- IFo=6e5: a 600,000 ms installation OAuth grace period.
- EFo registers pending installation state; jFo schedules NFo at expiry.
- NFo requests app/installed with forceRefresh=true and requires the matching app's callable flag.
- If verification does not establish readiness, it emits the plugin installation timeout notification and invokes OFo -> PFo -> dFo -> nFo, which sends plugin/uninstall.
- AFo restores pending reconciliation records on focus/visibility events.

Asset SHA-256: 712ac9f965de1a4c9cb75ae1c149cf25747da8056b8c32039dc1e2c43e3dc124.

This identifies the removal mechanism and explains the two timelines. It does not establish whether the earlier connection-state mismatch originates in the app callback, registry/bridge, or desktop reconciliation.

### What is the expected behavior?

A successfully installed plugin with a working authenticated MCP connection should not disappear because a separate app connection is still pending. Surface the precise missing connection and a recovery action. Preserve installed skills and the working MCP connection, or at minimum reconcile both auth lifecycles before destructive installation rollback.

### Additional information

Related: #44188 examines the same reconciliation path when connection-state queries throw. This report adds two real-world occurrences with successful MCP OAuth/API usage and app/installed requests returning errorCode=null; no query exception has been established here. Please merge if these are considered the same defect.

Temporary workaround: restoring the plugin with codex plugin add rather than the desktop install UI did not create a new frontend pending-install flow. At 618 seconds after restoration, the plugin remained installed and enabled. This is a short observation, not proof of a permanent fix.

No signed client files were modified. No full session transcript, OAuth URLs, access tokens, account/zone/tunnel identifiers, private hostnames, local usernames, or complete application logs are included.

labels.name: enhancement

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

Codex on macOS; evidence from local .codex JSONL session transcripts, with recorded cli_version values spanning 0.153.4–0.160.0.

### What feature would you like to see?

Please implement a persistent, cancellable capacity queue. When the selected model is temporarily overloaded, preserve the request and resume automatically when capacity returns. Do not terminate the turn and tell the user to choose another model.

The current message is:

> Selected model is at capacity. Please try a different model.

This is deeply frustrating and an unnecessarily poor design for an agent expected to carry out sustained work. Backend capacity management is the service’s responsibility. Making the user babysit a task, repeatedly resubmit it, or abandon their deliberately selected model is not a sensible recovery mechanism. I am happy to wait; I am not happy to have the request interrupted because the service is busy. A queue is basic backpressure handling, not an exotic feature.

Requested behavior:

- Treat server_overloaded as a recoverable queued state, not terminal task completion.
- Retain the selected model, pending request, conversation context, and completed tool results. Resume from the interrupted inference boundary rather than restarting the entire task.
- Show an honest “Waiting for model capacity; will resume automatically” status, with cancel and optional model-switch controls. Do not invent an ETA.
- Use bounded-backoff retries with jitter or server-side scheduling, rather than requiring another user message.
- Preserve pending-message ordering; do not skip the blocked request and execute dependent follow-ups.
- Persist the queue across reconnects/restarts, with clear cancellation semantics and no silent abandonment.
- Handle overload during remote compaction as recoverable too.
- Never replay completed external writes or bypass approval requirements when resuming. Model switching must be optional and explicit.

Acceptance criterion: a temporary capacity failure leaves the original request pending, and it continues on the same model without user intervention once capacity becomes available.

### Additional information

I searched local session and archived-session transcripts for the exact error text, then counted only structured event_msg / task_complete records whose error.message contains it, excluding user quotations, tool output, and this issue-writing session.

Found 34 matching error completions across 17 transcript files, dated September 12–October 2, 2026 (UTC). All matching completions report codex_error_info: server_overloaded. One is prefixed “Error running remote compact task:”.

Sanitized examples:

| Completion timestamp (UTC) | Recorded CLI version | Recorded turn duration before failure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2026-09-30T13:34:13.689Z | 0.155.1 | 9,091,706 ms (~151.5 minutes) |
| 2026-10-01T15:29:40.345Z | 0.159.3 | 6,357,258 ms (~105.9 minutes) |
| 2026-10-02T07:52:33.249Z | 0.159.3 | 4,321,373 ms (~72.0 minutes) |
| 2026-10-02T08:16:59.914Z | 0.160.0 | 258,000 ms (4.3 minutes) |
| 2026-10-02T08:22:08.931Z | 0.160.0 | 300,231 ms (~5.0 minutes) |

These are recorded turn durations, not measurements of time spent exclusively waiting for capacity. They demonstrate terminal capacity errors after substantial elapsed task time. This evidence does not establish the backend cause or how much work was lost.

Representative sanitized record:

```json
{
  "timestamp": "2026-10-02T08:22:08.931Z",
  "type": "event_msg",
  "payload": {
    "type": "task_complete",
    "last_agent_message": null,
    "error": {
      "message": "Selected model is at capacity. Please try a different model.",
      "codex_error_info": "server_overloaded"
    },
    "duration_ms": 300231
  }
}
```

Related requests: #31278 and #33853; related long-running-task interruption report: #41810. This issue adds repeated local transcript evidence and asks specifically for persistent queueing and safe continuation, including compaction, rather than terminal interruption. If consolidated, please retain this evidence and the queue/continuation acceptance criteria.

### Confirmed V8 out-of-memory crash captured live (2026-10-03 05:24:45 UTC)

This update supersedes the earlier model-only hypothesis and the earlier lack of a native dump. On the same app build, **Astra worked with microphone dictation in the diagnostic conversation and in a different project**. The other project's task finished before the affected conversation was tested.

The user then opened the large existing affected conversation and dictated with Astra selected. The renderer reset **during dictation, before Send**. No new text task was submitted in that reproduction.

**Native evidence**
- Desktop 26.930.31730, build 12947; MSIX 26.930.3930.0; Chromium 154.0.8037.98.
- Renderer PID 37976 exited at 05:24:45.238933 UTC (08:24:45.238933 Europe/Bucharest), with native status **0xE0000008**, Chromium's out-of-memory exception.
- A 3,730,544-byte Crashpad minidump was preserved locally before cleanup. The exception stream and chrome.dll Crashpad annotations were independently decoded.
- `v8-oom-location = MarkCompactCollector: young object promotion failed`
- `v8-oom-main-cage-last-alloc-status = ran out of reservation`
- `v8-oom-main-cage-size = 4096.00MB`
- `v8-oom-main-cage-free-size = 0B`
- `v8-oom-main-cage-largest-free-region = 0B`
- `v8-oom-is-main-isolate = true`; `v8-oom-last-os-error = 0`
- `v8-oom-lo-space-size = 2629.95MB`

**Live memory/process observations**
The renderer's private memory rose from approximately 809 MiB at 05:24:03 UTC to **5.63 GiB** at 05:24:37 UTC, with large fluctuations before exit. Windows still had at least **11.64 GiB physical memory available** and **10.77 GiB commit available** during the crash window. The main process and GPU process remained alive, and replacement renderers started at 05:24:45.56 UTC. This is confirmed V8 reservation exhaustion, not evidence of system-wide RAM exhaustion.

**History-size correlation; exact retained objects remain unknown**
The affected conversation has 51,857 stored UI items totaling 2,164,862,691 JSON characters; its rollout is 10,170,614,309 bytes. It already uses paginated history. Three individual historical turns total approximately 297M, 272M and 173M JSON characters. These are stored-history sizes, not a claim that all those bytes were loaded into RAM. Astra was stable in the diagnostic conversation (541 items) and the comparison project conversation (6,843 items). Excessive loading or retention of history is a strong investigation lead; the dump does not identify the responsible JavaScript objects or source line.

Please investigate and bound renderer history hydration/retention and large-item handling, including dictation/composer updates in existing conversations. **Recovery test update (05:47 UTC):** the user successfully dictated with Astra and submitted a message in a new, short-context conversation in the SAME project; the requested project audit then started. Live monitoring from approximately 05:43 to 05:47 UTC recorded no new renderer crash, with the same renderer staying alive and a peak private memory of about 0.965 GiB. This short successful test strengthens the conversation-history investigation lead, but does not establish long-term stability or repair the product bug. The original conversation and project files were preserved. No app binaries, GPU settings or history data were modified.

The native dump and private project/chat identifiers are retained locally or supplied through private support; they are not published here. Account-specific abnormal-usage review remains with private support.

Chromium definition of the exception: [oom.h](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/d9b8153d34deb93f08d6a61eb12b6cd04486dbd9/base/allocator/partition_allocator/src/partition_alloc/oom.h).

---

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

Installed application bundle: **26.928.20755**, build **12246**.
Bundle identifier: `com.openai.codex`.

### What subscription do you have?

Not specified in this report.

### What platform is your computer?

macOS **26.5** (build **25F71**), Apple Silicon.

```text
Darwin 25.5.0 arm64 arm
```

### What issue are you seeing?

With a side chat open, confirming a response annotation in the **main chat** moves keyboard focus to the **side-chat composer**.

The observed workflow is: main-chat response → add annotation → enter a note → confirm. The user then has to return focus to the main composer manually. Otherwise, subsequent typing may go into the wrong conversation.

This report concerns the focus destination. It does **not** establish that the annotation itself is saved to or sent to the wrong conversation.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

User-observed sequence:

1. Open a main Codex chat and keep a side chat open beside it.
2. In the main chat's assistant response, choose the response annotation action (“채팅에 주석 달기” in the Korean UI).
3. Enter an annotation and confirm it (“확인”).
4. Observe that focus moves to the side chat instead of staying in the main chat's workflow.

The code analysis below identifies a more specific condition to test: **focus the side-chat composer before step 2, then annotate the main response without first focusing the main composer**. This strengthened sequence is derived from the inspected routing logic; it has not been independently replayed end to end in the desktop UI. Merely having a side chat open is not proven sufficient in every state.

### What is the expected behavior?

Confirming an annotation originating from the main chat should return focus to the main chat's composer, or another appropriate control in that same workflow. It should not select another conversation's composer based on stale focus history.

### Additional information

#### Code inspection

The relevant desktop response-annotation frontend was not found in the public `openai/codex` checkout inspected at `14a477ea89712071944244022e8a10142845456e`. The following observations come from read-only inspection of the installed app's packaged JavaScript:

- `app-primary-92c16ff2fe4e.js`: the response-annotation confirm callback closes the editor with `restoreFocus: false`, updates the annotation, and calls `ay()` without an owning composer/thread argument.
- `ay` imports `H_n` from `app-initial-74096abaa6b3.js`, where that export is `SA`.
- `SA()` selects a composer through `CA()` and schedules its `.focus()`.
- `CA()` first returns `EA`, the last-focused registered composer, if it remains connected and registered. Only afterward does it fall back to the primary composer.
- Composer registration (`LSn`) updates `EA` on composer focus. Focusing the separate annotation editor does not itself register that editor as the main composer.

The confirm callback in this build is:

```js
e => {
  let t = R.annotation.id;
  H(t, { restoreFocus: false });
  l(t, e);
  ay();
}
```

These minified identifiers are specific to the inspected build.

#### Isolated verification and limitations

The actual extracted confirm callback and composer-selection/registration functions were executed in Node with simulated DOM elements, annotation-update callbacks, and animation-frame scheduling.

| Simulated state before confirming the main annotation | Focus after confirmation |
| --- | --- |
| Side composer was last focused and remains registered/connected | **Side composer** |
| Main composer was last focused | Main composer |
| Side composer was last focused but is disconnected | Main composer |
| No previous composer focus recorded | Main composer |

All four assertions passed. The simulated annotation-update callback retained the main annotation ID.

This is an isolated verification of the extracted routing logic, **not an automated desktop UI reproduction**. It supports a likely cause of the reported symptom but does not establish every runtime trigger, actual persistence behavior, or reproduction frequency.

A potential fix is to restore focus using the annotation's owning composer rather than the global last-focused composer. A regression test should cover a main-chat annotation while the side composer was last focused.

#### Related issues

- #39338 — “Add to chat” does not focus the composer after attaching selected response text.
- #43510 — opening inline review comments causes chat to take focus and the review pane to jump.

Those reports concern related focus behavior, but neither describes this main-response-annotation → side-chat focus transfer. A shared root cause has not been established.

items.body:
Codex in VS Code is a daily work tool for paying customers. Release reliability and timely handling of regressions directly affect their ability to work.

Version `26.928.31416` has reports of basic message submission breaking:

- [#49854](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/49854) reports follow-up messages stuck sending on Windows. The reporter says rolling back to `26.917.62051` restored message submission.
- [#49913](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/49913) reports prompts never submitting on Ubuntu.
- [#49834](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/49834) documents a JSON serialization defect in queued-message handling. Its relationship to all reported submission failures has not been established.

These reports warrant clarification of how core workflows are validated before release and how critical regressions are handled afterward.

Please clarify:

- **Release criteria:** What testing and promotion criteria separate Pre-Release from Release? How are message submission, follow-up messages, and queued-message handling validated across supported platforms?
- **Ownership and visibility:** Which team owns critical VS Code regressions? Where can users track investigation progress, affected versions, and the version containing a fix?
- **Recovery:** What is the supported path when an update breaks basic functionality, including rollback and version pinning?

The [contribution guidelines](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/docs/contributing.md) welcome bug reports and root-cause analyses but do not accept external patches. With fixes depending on the internal team, please also explain how community diagnoses are triaged and translated into timely fixes.

Users should be able to rely on the Release channel for daily work. When a regression prevents that, they need a visible response and a supported way to recover.

## Summary

On macOS, Codex Desktop's frontend becomes unresponsive when a large generated HTML report is opened in the built-in file editor after a task finishes. This interrupts the entire chat workflow, rather than only making the file viewer slow.

**Suspected cause: syntax highlighting/tokenization of a multi-million-character line on the renderer thread.** This is a hypothesis, not a profiler-confirmed diagnosis. I initially described this as “lint”; the performance concern is specifically the file editor's syntax highlighting/parsing. We have not established whether a diagnostics/lint service is involved.

## Environment

- Codex Desktop on macOS 27.0.1 (26A434), Apple Silicon / arm64.
- Exact Codex Desktop build: not captured.
- Trigger: opening a generated `.html` file in the built-in file editor, including an agent opening it automatically at the end of a task.

## Observed file characteristics

The affected report is a self-contained HTML report with an embedded JSON data block and inline JavaScript:

- File size: **5,948,464 bytes** (about **5.67 MiB**).
- Number of lines: **58**.
- Longest line: **3,027,552 characters**.
- Much of the data is serialized onto one line.

These measurements were taken from the actual file. The report contains private case data and is not attached. No private report contents are needed to describe the file structure.

## Steps leading to the issue

1. Generate a large self-contained HTML report containing a large single-line JSON data block.
2. At the end of the task, open the HTML in Codex's built-in file editor (in our workflow the agent used the app's file-opening capability).
3. The Codex frontend freezes/becomes unresponsive.

The user has observed this when opening large HTML files, including the report measured above. We have not yet isolated the exact size/line-length threshold, collected a renderer CPU profile, or performed a controlled editor-versus-browser comparison.

## Expected behavior

Opening a large generated report should not freeze the entire Codex UI. In particular:

- Apply file-size and **maximum-line-length** limits before syntax highlighting.
- Fall back to plain text or offer an explicit “Open without syntax highlighting” action.
- Provide a per-file or global switch to disable file-editor highlighting/diagnostics, if none is currently available.
- Run expensive tokenization off the UI thread with cancellation and a timeout.
- Avoid automatically restoring a file editor tab that previously caused a renderer hang; offer a safe way to close/reset that tab.

Opening HTML as a rendered page in an external browser can avoid the built-in source editor, but that does not fix the editor reliability issue. We have not verified that workaround for this particular freeze.

## Related reports

items.title: Codex Desktop 26.930 generates malformed mixed Windows/WSL cwd, causing CreateProcess failures and unreadable attachments

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: tool-calls
labels.description: Issues related to tool calling

labels.name: app

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.930.21537

### What subscription do you have?

Plus

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26100.0 x64

### What issue are you seeing?

Codex Desktop 26.930.2377.0 still generates an invalid mixed Windows/WSL working-directory path for a project located inside WSL.

The issue reproduces in both existing conversations and newly created chats inside the same WSL project.

It also appears to affect file-attachment ingestion: prompts attached as `.txt` or `.md` files cannot be reliably read when the local process launcher fails, while the exact same prompt works when pasted inline into the chat.

## Environment

- Codex Desktop: `26.930.21537`
- Host OS: Windows
- WSL distribution: `Ubuntu-24.04`
- Agent environment: `Windows Subsystem for Linux`
- Integrated terminal shell: WSL
- Workspace: `/home/user/torbaretail_audit`

## Current application path

The currently installed Codex Desktop build runs from:
`C:\Program Files\WindowsApps\OpenAI.Codex_26.930.2377.0_x64__2p2nqsd0c76g0\app`

However, Codex still generates a command containing the path of an older Codex build (26.915.4065.0) and combines it with a WSL UNC path:
`cd '/mnt/c/Program Files/WindowsApps/OpenAI.Codex_26.915.4065.0_x64__2p2nqsd0c76g0/app/resources/\\wsl$\Ubuntu-24.04\home\user\torbaretail_audit'`

PowerShell then resolves this into the invalid path:
`C:\mnt\c\Program Files\WindowsApps\OpenAI.Codex_26.915.4065.0_x64__2p2nqsd0c76g0\app\resources\wsl$\Ubuntu-24.04\home\user\torbaretail_audit`

and fails with: `PathNotFound`

In other runs, the same underlying execution problem appears as:
`CreateProcess: No such file or directory (os error 2)`

WSL workspace itself is healthy. The workspace works normally when accessed directly through WSL:
`wsl -d Ubuntu-24.04`

Then inside WSL:
`cd /home/user/torbaretail_audit`
`pwd`

returns:
`/home/user/torbaretail_audit`

So the WSL distribution and the workspace itself are accessible.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Open Codex Desktop.
2. Use a project whose workspace is inside WSL:
`/home/user/<project>`
3. Set the Agent Environment to Windows Subsystem for Linux.
4. Open either:
- an existing chat in the project, or
- a newly created chat in the same project.

5. Ask Codex to execute a simple local command such as `pwd`.
6. Observe that Codex attempts to construct a working directory using a mixture of:
- a WindowsApps application path,
- a Linux /mnt/c/... path,
- and a \\wsl$\... UNC path.

The command fails before normal WSL execution begins.

### What is the expected behavior?

**Expected behavior**
For a WSL workspace, Codex should execute in the configured WSL environment with a Linux-native cwd such as:
`/home/user/torbaretail_audit`

It should not prepend a Windows application resource directory or translate the WSL workspace through a mixed Windows/Linux/UNC path.
Updating Codex Desktop should also not leave execution metadata pointing to an older WindowsApps package version.

**Actual behavior**
About / application build: `26.930.21537`

Current Windows package: `26.930.2377.0`

Stale package referenced by malformed command: `26.915.4065.0`

The currently installed application is: `26.930.2377.0` but the generated execution path still references: `26.915.4065.0` and combines that stale application path with the WSL workspace path. This suggests that stale pre-update execution/cwd metadata may be involved, together with incorrect WSL path canonicalization. I cannot confirm the exact root cause.

### Additional information

There appears to be another user-visible consequence correlated with the same process-launch failure.

If I send a new Codex prompt as a file attachment, for example a `.txt` or `.md` file, Codex is unable to reliably read the attachment.
Codex reports: `Local process launcher repeats transient CreateProcess: No such file or directory, so I will not make assumptions about the attachment contents.`

As a result, I have to paste the exact same prompt directly into the chat as inline text. When pasted inline, Codex can read and follow it normally. So the problem appears to affect not only terminal execution but also local file/attachment ingestion in WSL projects when Codex needs the local execution or workspace layer to access the attachment.

I cannot confirm that the attachment failure has exactly the same root cause, but it consistently occurs together with the same CreateProcess /
malformed-workspace-path failure.

The issue is not limited to restoring an old conversation. It also reproduces in a newly created chat inside the same WSL project.
